# Locality Guide: Javorje nad Škofjo Loko, Slovenia (c. 1812)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Historical name:** Bischoflack, Krain (Carniola), Austria — the FamilySearch Catalog records this area under "Bischoflack (Krain)"
- **Modern municipality:** Škofja Loka, Slovenia
- **Religious affiliation:** Roman Catholic (Archdiocese of Ljubljana)

---

## The Short Answer

For an 1812 marriage, search the **Roman Catholic parish marriage register** for whichever parish served Javorje. Those registers were kept in Latin, following a tabular format adopted in 1770/1784 under Emperor Joseph II.

**Important caveat:** The specific parish that covered Javorje nad Škofjo Loko in 1812 is not confirmed by this survey — identifying the serving parish is the essential first step.

---

## Where to Look

### 1. Matricula Online *(start here)*
- **URL:** https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/
- Hosts images of Slovenia Catholic church records; this is the primary online source for Slovenian parish registers
- Search there for the relevant parish's marriage register once the parish is identified

### 2. FamilySearch Catalog
- Search under "Škofja Loka" or the historical name "Bischoflack, Krain, Austria"
- 36 catalog items exist for this area; two items are confirmed online:
  - *Kirchliche Angelegenheiten 1550–1747* (koha:422727, film 1416653) — church documents for the area
  - *Knjiga hiš v Škofji Loki* by France Štukl (koha:502892, film 1183591) — a compiled book of houses and inhabitants; FamilySearch Library only, not online
- **Note:** The FamilySearch volume search returned **0 digitized volumes** for Škofja Loka for 1790–1830, confirming the parish registers are not in FamilySearch's main image database for this period

### 3. Archdiocesan Archive in Ljubljana *(for originals or parish identification)*
- **Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana**
- Krekov trg 1, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia
- Email: arhiv.lj@rkc.si
- Holds original pre-1880s parish registers for the Archdiocese of Ljubljana

---

## Key Facts for 1812

- **Civil registration did not yet exist** — only the Catholic parish register records this marriage; no civil marriage record exists for this date
- **No duplicate registers in 1812** — civil duplicate registers were not mandated until 1835 (Catholic) and 1829 (Evangelical), so only the parish's own copy of the marriage entry exists
- **Record language:** Latin
- **Status animarum** (household lists of parishioners, extant from 1750) can supplement the marriage register if the entry is hard to find

---

## Record Losses

No tool result reports destruction or loss of parish registers for the Škofja Loka area. The absence of digitized volumes in FamilySearch for this date range is a **coverage gap**, not a confirmed loss.

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Contact the Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana** (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) to identify which parish served Javorje c. 1812
2. **Search that parish's marriage register on Matricula Online** (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/)
3. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog** directly for additional holdings under "Škofja Loka" and "Bischoflack"

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City | Knjiga hiš v Škofji Loki (film 1183591); other Škofja Loka films | In-person or FamilySearch Library loan |

## Records NOT online

- The FamilySearch volume search found no digitized volumes for Škofja Loka in 1790–1830, confirming the registers are not in FamilySearch's main image database for this period and place

## Known record losses
No tool result reports destruction or loss of parish registers for the Škofja Loka area. The absence of digitized volumes for this date range is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss.

## Research tips
- **Start with Matricula Online** (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/): the FamilySearch Slovenia Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Slovenia_Church_Records) names this as the online home for Slovenia church record images; it is the first place to look for the 1812 marriage register
- **Identify the serving parish before searching:** The specific parish that covered Javorje in 1812 is not confirmed by any tool result; contacting the Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana (arhiv.lj@rkc.si) to establish the parish assignment is a necessary first step before ordering records
- **Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly** for the remaining 32 items filed under Škofja Loka (https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) — the catalog found 36 total items but this survey only detailed 4
- **Records are in Latin:** Marriage entries in Catholic parish registers from 1812 follow the tabular format introduced in 1770/1784; the researcher must be able to read Latin or obtain a translation
- **Status animarum as a supplement:** If the marriage register entry is hard to locate, the status animarum (household list of parishioners, extant from 1750) may confirm the family's presence and date range in the parish (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Slovenia_Church_Records)
- **Duplicate registers were not yet required in 1812:** Civil duplicate registers were mandated only in 1835 (Catholic) and 1829 (Evangelical), so only the parish's own copy of the marriage entry exists for 1812 — the archdiocesan archive is the definitive repository

---

For an 1812 marriage in Javorje nad Škofjo Loko, the record would have been made in the Catholic parish marriage register for whichever parish served that small village in Carniola. Those pre-1880 original registers are held at the Archdiocese of Ljubljana's archive in Ljubljana (Nadškofijski arhiv, email: arhiv.lj@rkc.si), and images of Slovenian Catholic church records are available to browse online at Matricula Online (https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/). The most important warning is that this survey could not confirm which specific parish covered Javorje in 1812 — establishing that parish assignment by contacting the archive directly is the essential first step before searching any register.

The next step is to contact the Nadškofijski arhiv Ljubljana to identify the serving parish for Javorje c. 1812, then search that parish's marriage register on Matricula Online.

# Locality Guide: Kolonica, Slovakia (1700–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Historical name:** Kolonicza (Hungarian)
- **Administrative center during target period:** Sátoraljaújhely (seat of Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary)
- **Parent jurisdiction during target period:** Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary (Habsburg Empire)
- **Modern location:** Snina District, northeastern Slovakia
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this village
- **Economy:** Primarily subsistence agriculture in a Rusyn/Ruthenian peasant community
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Rusyn (Ruthenian/Ukrainian-descended) population
- **Religious denominations:** Greek Catholic (confirmed as parish denomination by FamilySearch catalog entry koha:727653); Roman Catholic and other denominations may have served nobles or administrators, but no other-denomination records were found in this survey
- **Key historical events:** Entirely within Habsburg Hungary throughout the 1700–1890 target period; transferred to Czechoslovakia in 1918

## Boundary changes
- During the entire target period (1700–1890), Kolonica was in Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary. Records from this era use the Hungarian name Kolonicza.
- After World War I (1918), the village became part of Czechoslovakia under Snina District. Administrative re-assignments followed in 1960, 1993, and 1996 within Czechoslovakia/Slovakia.
- For research before 1918, search under the Hungarian county jurisdiction Zemplén; for 1918 onward, search under Czechoslovakia or Slovakia as appropriate.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Slovakia-specific vital records pages during this survey; no specific year for civil registration can be cited from tool results for this jurisdiction.
- **What exists:** Greek Catholic church registers served as the de facto vital records throughout the entire 1700–1890 target period. See Church records below.
- **Where held:** Originals at the Štátny archív v Levoči (State Archive in Levoča), Slovakia — confirmed as the microfilm source in catalog entry koha:727653.
- **Gaps:** No confirmed civil registration records for the target period; church registers are the primary source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Greek Catholic parish (Grécko-katolícka cirkev, Farský úrad Kolonica) confirmed by catalog entry koha:727653. No records for other denominations were found in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (Krsty), Marriages (Manželstvá), Deaths (Úmrtia) — confirmed from catalog entry koha:727653.
- **Where held — originals:** Štátny archív v Levoči (State Archive in Levoča), Slovakia; original documents microfilmed there (catalog entry koha:727653).
- **Where held — online (name-indexed):** FamilySearch Slovakia Church and Synagogue Books collection (https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443). Images from films 1792766 and 1792767 are available and name-indexed.
- **Confirmed online coverage:**
  - Film 1792766 (image group 4406755, Granite Mountain Record Vault): Baptisms 1824–1833; Marriages 1825–1833; Deaths 1824–1833; Baptisms 1890–1922
  - Film 1792767 (image group 4405907, FamilySearch Library): Baptisms 1922–1924 (continued); Marriages 1890–1924; Deaths 1890–1924
- **Gaps:**
  - No church records before 1824 were found for Kolonica in the FamilySearch catalog. For the 1700s through 1823, no Kolonica-specific registers have been confirmed by this survey.
  - Film 1793684 is noted in the catalog as part of this register collection but its images are not available online (catalog entry koha:727653). This film likely covers the period approximately 1834–1889 for marriages, deaths, and possibly baptisms, for which no online images appear in the confirmed coverage above. Contact the Štátny archív v Levoči or request the film through the FamilySearch Library to access this period.
  - There is therefore a confirmed gap in online images for approximately 1834–1889 and no confirmed records at all before 1824.
- **Language:** Latin and Hungarian (catalog entry koha:727653). Latin predominates in the earlier registers; Hungarian becomes prevalent in the mid-to-late 19th century.

### Census records
- **1869 Zemplén County census:** The Népszámlálás (census) of Zemplén County, 1869, includes Kolonica under the Hungarian name Kolonicza. Film 722725 (image group 8144603) covers the entry and is available online at the Slovakia Census, 1869 collection (https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1986782). The original was microfilmed at the Magyar Országos Levéltár (Hungarian National Archives) in Budapest (catalog entry koha:385993). Localities are listed alphabetically by Hungarian name; Slovakia-portion images are online.
- **Earlier Habsburg censuses:** No Habsburg-era census records for Kolonica specifically (such as the 1850 or 1857 Austrian census, or the 1770s conscription/konskription) were found in this survey's catalog search.
- **Access:** The 1869 census is online and browsable; name-index status is not confirmed from catalog notes.

### Probate and court records
- No probate or court records for Kolonica were found in this survey. Such records for Zemplén County would have been created at the county level and are likely held at the Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár (Hungarian National Archives) or its Zemplén County branch (now in Sátoraljaújhely, Hungary), or at the Štátny archív v Prešove (State Archive in Prešov, Slovakia) for the Slovak portion.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes-and-bounds style land descriptions were used in Hungarian-era records.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land in Zemplén County during the target period was held under the Hungarian feudal/estate system. No specific land-distribution office holdings for Kolonica were confirmed by tool results in this survey.
- **Types:** Urbarial registers (surveys of serf obligations) were conducted periodically in Habsburg Hungary from the mid-18th century and may cover Kolonica. These records are potentially held in Hungarian archives; this survey did not confirm specific Kolonica holdings.
- **Where held:** Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár or its county branch; possibly also Štátny archív v Prešove for Slovak-side Zemplén records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Seven Years' War (1756–1763), Napoleonic Wars (early 1800s), and various Habsburg campaigns throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Habsburg conscription (Konskription) lists, possibly from the 1770s onward; military service records.
- **Where held:** Österreichisches Staatsarchiv (Austrian State Archives), Vienna, for Habsburg imperial military records; Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár for Hungarian army records.

### Cemetery records
- No cemetery databases specifically covering Kolonica were confirmed in this survey. The primary burial record source is the Deaths (Úmrtia) series in the Greek Catholic registers (film 1792766 and 1792767 for confirmed online periods).

### Newspaper records
- No local newspaper records for Kolonica were confirmed. As a small rural village, Kolonica would not have had its own newspaper. Regional newspapers of Zemplén County may carry occasional legal or military notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- Emigration from northeastern Slovakia (Zemplén County) to the United States was substantial from the late 19th century onward, particularly to Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey coal and steel regions. Naturalization petitions, passenger arrival manifests, and alien registration records for emigrants are held at NARA and are searchable through FamilySearch (free), Ancestry, and other online repositories.
- Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family's emigration, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- Urbarial registers (surveys of serf obligations and land holdings) were conducted periodically in Habsburg Hungary from roughly the 1760s. For Zemplén County, these records may cover Kolonica and serve as a substitute for the missing pre-1824 church records. This survey did not confirm specific Kolonica urbarial records in the FamilySearch catalog; they are likely held in Hungarian archives.

### Other record types
- **Canonical visitation records (Visitationes Canonicae):** Periodic church inspections of Greek Catholic parishes sometimes recorded village population lists and can predate surviving parish registers. For the Diocese of Mukachevo (which held authority over Kolonica before 1818), these records would be in Ukraine (Uzhhorod or Mukachevo eparchial archives). After 1818 they fall under the Greek Catholic Diocese of Prešov archive. This survey cannot confirm specific Kolonica entries in those archives.
- **Estate and domain records:** The noble estate that controlled Kolonica may have kept household or labor records. These would be in Hungarian county or estate archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch — Slovakia Church and Synagogue Books (https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443) | Greek Catholic parish registers, Kolonica 1824–1833 and 1890–1924, name-indexed (catalog entry koha:727653) | Pre-civil-registration vital records | Free |
| FamilySearch — Slovakia Census, 1869 (https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1986782) | 1869 Zemplén County census including Kolonicza (Kolonica), film 722725 (catalog entry koha:385993) | Census records for the target period | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch collections search and volume search returned no results for this place (place resolution failed for those tools). The two collections above were identified through the FamilySearch Catalog. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Slovakia returned only generic content; Slovakia-specific guidance pages could not be confirmed through the tools.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Štátny archív v Levoči (State Archive in Levoča), Slovakia | Originals of Greek Catholic parish registers for Kolonica, 1824–1924, confirmed as microfilm source (catalog entry koha:727653) | In-person or written inquiry |
| Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár (Hungarian National Archives), Budapest | Original 1869 Zemplén County census (catalog entry koha:385993); county-level probate, land, and administrative records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Štátny archív v Prešove (State Archive in Prešov), Slovakia | Additional Zemplén County records for the Slovak portion; Greek Catholic Diocese of Prešov records (post-1818) | In-person or written inquiry |
| Greek Catholic Eparchial Archive, Uzhhorod / Mukachevo, Ukraine | Possibly holds canonical visitation records and diocesan materials for the period before 1818 (Diocese of Mukachevo era) | Contact archive directly |

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Administrative center during target period:** Sátoraljaújhely (seat of Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary)
- **Parent jurisdiction during target period:** Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary (Habsburg Empire)
- **Modern location:** Snina District, northeastern Slovakia
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this village
- **Economy:** Primarily subsistence agriculture in a Rusyn/Ruthenian peasant community
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Rusyn (Ruthenian/Ukrainian-descended) population
- **Religious denominations:** Greek Catholic (confirmed as parish denomination by FamilySearch catalog entry koha:727653); Roman Catholic and other denominations may have served nobles or administrators, but no other-denomination records were found in this survey
- **Key historical events:** Entirely within Habsburg Hungary throughout the 1700–1890 target period; transferred to Czechoslovakia in 1918

## Boundary changes
- During the entire target period (1700–1890), Kolonica was in Zemplén County, Kingdom of Hungary. Records from this era use the Hungarian name Kolonicza.
- After World War I (1918), the village became part of Czechoslovakia under Snina District. Administrative re-assignments followed in 1960, 1993, and 1996 within Czechoslovakia/Slovakia.
- For research before 1918, search under the Hungarian county jurisdiction Zemplén; for 1918 onward, search under Czechoslovakia or Slovakia as appropriate.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Slovakia-specific vital records pages during this survey; no specific year for civil registration can be cited from tool results for this jurisdiction.
- **What exists:** Greek Catholic church registers served as the de facto vital records throughout the entire 1700–1890 target period. See Church records below.
- **Where held:** Originals at the Štátny archív v Levoči (State Archive in Levoča), Slovakia — confirmed as the microfilm source in catalog entry koha:727653.
- **Gaps:** No confirmed civil registration records for the target period; church registers are the primary source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Greek Catholic parish (Grécko-katolícka cirkev, Farský úrad Kolonica) confirmed by catalog entry koha:727653. No records for other denominations were found in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (Krsty), Marriages (Manželstvá), Deaths (Úmrtia) — confirmed from catalog entry koha:727653.
- **Where held — originals:** Štátny archív v Levoči (State Archive in Levoča), Slovakia; original documents microfilmed there (catalog entry koha:727653).
- **Where held — online (name-indexed):** FamilySearch Slovakia Church and Synagogue Books collection (https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1554443). Images from films 1792766 and 1792767 are available and name-indexed.
- **Confirmed online coverage:**
  - Film 1792766 (image group 4406755, Granite Mountain Record Vault): Baptisms 1824–1833; Marriages 1825–1833; Deaths 1824–1833; Baptisms 1890–1922
  - Film 1792767 (image group 4405907, FamilySearch Library): Baptisms 1922–1924 (continued); Marriages 1890–1924; Deaths 1890–1924
- **Gaps:**

Contact the Štátny archív v Levoči or request the film through the FamilySearch Library to access this period.
  - There is therefore a confirmed gap in online images for approximately 1834–1889 and no confirmed records at all before 1824.
- **Language:** Latin and Hungarian (catalog entry koha:727653). Latin predominates in the earlier registers; Hungarian becomes prevalent in the mid-to-late 19th century.

### Census records
- **1869 Zemplén County census:** The Népszámlálás (census) of Zemplén County, 1869, includes Kolonica under the Hungarian name Kolonicza. Film 722725 (image group 8144603) covers the entry and is available online at the Slovakia Census, 1869 collection (https://familysearch.org/search/collection/1986782). The original was microfilmed at the Magyar Országos Levéltár (Hungarian National Archives) in Budapest (catalog entry koha:385993). Localities are listed alphabetically by Hungarian name; Slovakia-portion images are online.
- **Earlier Habsburg censuses:** No Habsburg-era census records for Kolonica specifically (such as the 1850 or 1857 Austrian census, or the 1770s conscription/konskription) were found in this survey's catalog search.
- **Access:** The 1869 census is online and browsable; name-index status is not confirmed from catalog notes.

### Probate and court records
- No probate or court records for Kolonica were found in this survey. Such records for Zemplén County would have been created at the county level and are likely held at the Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár (Hungarian National Archives) or its Zemplén County branch (now in Sátoraljaújhely, Hungary), or at the Štátny archív v Prešove (State Archive in Prešov, Slovakia) for the Slovak portion.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes-and-bounds style land descriptions were used in Hungarian-era records.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land in Zemplén County during the target period was held under the Hungarian feudal/estate system. No specific land-distribution office holdings for Kolonica were confirmed by tool results in this survey.
- **Types:** Urbarial registers (surveys of serf obligations) were conducted periodically in Habsburg Hungary from the mid-18th century and may cover Kolonica. These records are potentially held in Hungarian archives; this survey did not confirm specific Kolonica holdings.
- **Where held:** Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár or its county branch; possibly also Štátny archív v Prešove for Slovak-side Zemplén records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Seven Years' War (1756–1763), Napoleonic Wars (early 1800s), and various Habsburg campaigns throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Habsburg conscription (Konskription) lists, possibly from the 1770s onward; military service records.
- **Where held:** Österreichisches Staatsarchiv (Austrian State Archives), Vienna, for Habsburg imperial military records; Magyar Nemzeti Levéltár for Hungarian army records.

### Cemetery records
- No cemetery databases specifically covering Kolonica were confirmed in this survey. The primary burial record source is the Deaths (Úmrtia) series in the Greek Catholic registers (film 1792766 and 1792767 for confirmed online periods).

### Newspaper records
- No local newspaper records for Kolonica were confirmed. As a small rural village, Kolonica would not have had its own newspaper. Regional newspapers of Zemplén County may carry occasional legal or military notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- Emigration from northeastern Slovakia (Zemplén County) to the United States was substantial from the late 19th century onward, particularly to Pennsylvania, New York, and New Jersey coal and steel regions. Naturalization petitions, passenger arrival manifests, and alien registration records for emigrants are held at NARA and are searchable through FamilySearch (free), Ancestry, and other online repositories.
- Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family's emigration, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- Urbarial registers (surveys of serf obligations and land holdings) were conducted periodically in Habsburg Hungary from roughly the 1760s. For Zemplén County, these records may cover Kolonica and serve as a substitute for the missing pre-1824 church records. This survey did not confirm specific Kolonica urbarial records in the FamilySearch catalog; they are likely held in Hungarian archives.

For the Diocese of Mukachevo (which held authority over Kolonica before 1818), these records would be in Ukraine (Uzhhorod or Mukachevo eparchial archives). After 1818 they fall under the Greek Catholic Diocese of Prešov archive. This survey cannot confirm specific Kolonica entries in those archives.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761, carved from Hampshire County
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Borders:** New York State (Columbia and Rensselaer counties) to the west; Vermont (Bennington County) to the north
- **Economy:** Farming, paper mills, iron forges, and textile mills; Housatonic River valley was the industrial spine
- **Religion:** Congregational (dominant), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker, and Catholic (arriving with Irish immigrants in the 1840s)

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**The town is the vital-records unit in Massachusetts.** Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded at the town level (not the county level) under a mandate dating to 1639. Statewide collection began only in 1841, so for 1820–1840 you must work town-by-town.

**Key sources:**

- **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" published series** — The fastest entry point. These transcribed volumes exist for most Berkshire County towns and are held at NEHGS, many public libraries, and reproduced on Ancestry. Start here.
- **FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (collection 2061550) — Online at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)
- **FamilySearch browse-only image volume** (image group 004500891, 512 images) — Covers Berkshire County town clerk vital records, 1761–1850. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable**; it must be browsed image by image.
- **Massachusetts state vital records (from 1841):** Copies submitted to the state beginning 1841. No statewide index covers 1820–1840.

**Marriage intentions** were recorded separately in the bride's (and sometimes the groom's) home town — check both towns when searching a marriage.

---

## Church Records

A critical complement to civil vital records, especially before 1841.

- **FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection 1921657) — Online at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)
- **FamilySearch browse-only volume** (image group 004500892, 274 images) — Pittsfield Congregational church records, 1791–1850. Browse-only, no name index.
- For other denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker), contact the individual congregation or its denominational archive — these are largely not in an online index for this period.

---

## Census Records

| Year | Coverage | Named members |
|------|----------|---------------|
| 1820 | Berkshire County | Head of household only |
| 1830 | Berkshire County | Head of household only |
| 1840 | Berkshire County | Head of household only |
| 1850 | Berkshire County | **Every household member** |

All four censuses are indexed and available at FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1850 mortality schedule (persons who died in the year before the enumeration) also accompanies the 1850 census.

**Tax lists as a census substitute:** Town tax valuation lists can substitute for census years, particularly 1820–1840. Held at town clerks' offices and the Massachusetts Archives (Boston); not comprehensively online.

---

## Probate and Land Records

- **Probate:** Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield, from 1761. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection 1678901) at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901).
- **Land/Deeds:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield, from 1761. Massachusetts used a metes-and-bounds survey system (not federal land states); deeds are at the county level.

---

## Military Records

- **War of 1812** (1812–1815) and **Mexican-American War** (1846–1848) service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are at NARA — accessible via [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) and the [National Archives](https://www.archives.gov/).
- Massachusetts militia records are at the Massachusetts Archives, Boston.

---

## Other Sources

- **Newspapers:** The *Pittsfield Sun* and *Berkshire American* carried marriage and death notices. Available via [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Cemetery records:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) for Berkshire County; coverage varies by town.
- **Naturalization:** FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213).

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Individual town clerks (each Berkshire town) | Original vital records, 1820–1850 | Contact town clerk directly |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deeds from 1761 | In-person or written request |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Probate files from 1761 | In-person or written request |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | State vital records from 1841; militia/military; tax lists | In-person; some online |
| NEHGS, Boston | "Vital Records to 1850" series; compiled genealogies; Berkshire-specific collections | Membership for online; in-person in Boston |
| FamilySearch | Town vitals, church records, probate, naturalization, census | Free — familysearch.org |

---

## Critical Research Tip: Search Across State Lines

Because your family's town is near both the New York and Vermont lines:

- A family in a **northern Berkshire town** (Adams, Williamstown, Florida) is a short distance from **Bennington County, Vermont**.
- A family in a **western or southwestern town** (Hancock, Richmond, Alford, Egremont, Sheffield) is close to **Columbia County, New York**.

Vital records, deeds, probate, and church membership could appear on either side of those borders. Search neighboring jurisdictions in parallel.

---

## Where to Start

1. Identify the specific Berkshire town your family lived in.
2. Search that town's entry in the **"Vital Records of [Town] to 1850"** published series.
3. Search FamilySearch collection **2061550** (Massachusetts Town Vital Records).
4. If nothing turns up, browse the unindexed image volume **004500891** page by page.
5. Search church records (collection 1921657; browse volume 004500892 for Pittsfield Congregational).
6. Search the 1820–1850 federal censuses on FamilySearch or Ancestry.
7. If the town is near the NY or VT border, run parallel searches in those neighboring counties.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761, carved from Hampshire County
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts (Commonwealth)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tool for this county; consult published census tabulations for 1820–1850
- **Economy:** Farming, early paper mills, iron forges, and textile mills; the Housatonic River valley was the industrial spine
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended Yankee families in this period, with small numbers of Irish immigrants beginning to arrive by the late 1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (dominant), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker (particularly in the southern towns), and Catholic (appearing in the 1840s with Irish immigration)
- **Key historical events:** War of 1812 disrupted local trade; canal and early railroad construction in the 1830s–1840s; growth of mill towns (Adams, North Adams, Pittsfield)

## Boundary changes

- Berkshire County was formed from Hampshire County in 1761 and its external borders have been stable since. No internal boundary changes within the county affect the 1820–1850 period.
- The county borders New York State directly to the west (Columbia and Rensselaer counties, NY) and Vermont to the north (Bennington County, VT). A family living in a northern or western Berkshire town very likely generated records on both sides of those lines.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start dates:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by Massachusetts law as early as 1639, so individual town clerks were creating these records well before 1820. Statewide (Commonwealth-level) registration began in 1841; Boston lagged and was not fully reporting to the state system until 1850. Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** Births, marriages (and separately, marriage intentions), and deaths held at the town level for the entire 1820–1850 period. For 1841–1850, copies were also submitted to the state.
- **Marriage intentions:** Recorded separately in the bride's home town; a parallel entry may also appear in the groom's home town and their current residence. Check both towns when searching a marriage. Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)
- **Where held:** Originals remain with each individual town clerk (Pittsfield, Lenox, Stockbridge, Great Barrington, Adams, Williamstown, etc.). The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, covering 3,456,789 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 and covers much of this period.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004500891 (512 images) covers Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850. It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- **Published transcriptions:** The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series covers more than 200 Massachusetts towns, including Berkshire County towns. These published volumes are a heavily used finding aid and are held at NEHGS, many public libraries, and reproduced on Ancestry. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)
- **Gaps:** Compliance with the 1639 mandate varied by town; some early entries are missing. The state system was absent before 1841, so statewide indexes do not cover 1820–1840.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational was the established church in Massachusetts through disestablishment in 1833 and is the most heavily documented. Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker, and (by the 1840s) Catholic congregations also operated in Berkshire County.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and membership lists. Church records are the primary alternative source for vital events, especially before 1841.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records), online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 004500892 (274 images) covers Congregational church records for Pittsfield, Berkshire County, 1791–1850. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.
- **Where held:** Denominational records are held by individual congregations, by district or state-level denominational archives, and in many cases by the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) or Massachusetts Archives. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts Church Records returned only generic content during this survey; re-run the locality guide before relying on their absence.
- **Language:** English throughout this period.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 censuses all cover Berkshire County. The 1850 census is the first to name every household member; 1820–1840 name only household heads. All are indexed and available at FamilySearch, Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/), and other online repositories.
- **State/provincial census:** Massachusetts did not conduct a state census in this period that would fill the intercensal gaps; this survey did not confirm one for 1820–1850.
- **Other enumerations:** Town tax valuation lists exist and can substitute for census years. The mortality schedule accompanies the 1850 federal census (persons who died in the year before the enumeration).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories, guardianships; also naturalization records filed in the Court of Common Pleas and Superior Court.
- **Date range:** Berkshire County Probate Court records run from the county's formation in 1761. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records) is at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901.
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield. Physical records remain at the courthouse; the FamilySearch collection provides online coverage.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection 1459213, 345,678 records) is at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213 and covers Berkshire County filings.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state; land was not distributed through the federal General Land Office).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, and related instruments recorded at the county level. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey; specific details about the county recorder's holdings could not be confirmed from that source.
- **Date range:** Deeds for Berkshire County run from 1761 at the county level; the wiki_search result for Massachusetts Genealogy states that land records (deeds) survive in "remarkably complete runs" from the 1630s statewide. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield (originals).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (service 1812–1815); Black Hawk War and other smaller conflicts of the 1820s–1840s; Mexican-American War (1846–1848).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants for War of 1812 and later conflicts are held at the National Archives (NARA), accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and NARA directly (https://www.archives.gov/). State adjutant general records for Massachusetts militia are at the Massachusetts Archives. The wiki_search result notes that pre-1812 colonial militia rolls are at the Massachusetts Archives and partially published. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online index for Berkshire County cemeteries; coverage is volunteer-contributed and varies by town.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive are held by individual town governments or churches.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Berkshire County had active local newspapers in this period, including the Pittsfield Sun and Berkshire American. These carried marriage and death notices and legal notices.
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper digitization is available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/). The Library of Congress Chronicling America project may also hold issues.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** Berkshire County is not a port-of-entry county; it is inland. Nonetheless, declarations of intention (first papers), naturalization petitions, and alien registrations were filed in Berkshire County courts for immigrants who settled there. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (collection 1459213) covers these.
- **Passenger lists:** For the small number of foreign-born residents arriving during this period, passenger lists are held at NARA and indexed in the FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312, 1,234,567 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312, covering arrivals at Boston and other Massachusetts ports.
- **Content note:** Arrival manifests record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching families who immigrated.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town and county valuation (property) lists, poll taxes.
- **Substitute value:** Town tax lists can substitute for census years, particularly for 1820–1840 when the federal census named only heads of household. They are especially useful to confirm residence between censuses.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Massachusetts Archives (Boston). The FamilySearch Wiki pages covering Massachusetts tax records returned only generic content during this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (collection 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (collection 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (collection 1678901); Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (collection 1459213); Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (collection 1784312); browse-only volumes 004500891 (Town Clerk Vital, Berkshire Co.) and 004500892 (Pittsfield Congregational) | Town vitals, church records, probate, naturalization | Free — https://www.familysearch.org |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 census with name indexing | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Berkshire County graves not in a town clerk series | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Death and marriage notices not in vital record series | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records | War of 1812 and Mexican-American War service | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA (National Archives) | Federal records | Service records, pension files, naturalization originals | Free to query; copies by request — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Berkshire County in this period, and both were included above — the returned page is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Individual town clerks (each Berkshire town) | Original vital records (births, marriages, deaths, marriage intentions) for 1820–1850 | Contact each town clerk's office directly; some records are on FamilySearch microfilm |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deeds and land instruments from 1761 | In-person or written request |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Probate files from 1761 | In-person or written request |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony and state records; militia/military; state vital records from 1841 | In-person; some records online |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest regional genealogical library; "Vital Records to 1850" series; compiled genealogies | Membership for online access; in-person at Boston |
| Local Berkshire County congregations and denominational archives | Church registers not yet microfilmed or digitized | Contact individual churches or their denominational archives |

## Records NOT online

- Original vital records held by individual town clerks, beyond what FamilySearch collection 2061550 and browse volume 004500891 cover, are not comprehensively online and may require contacting the town clerk directly.
- Town tax valuation lists for most Berkshire towns in 1820–1850 are not in an online index; they require an in-person or written visit to the Massachusetts Archives or town clerk.
- Berkshire County court minute books (county business, road maintenance records, poor-relief records) are not known to be online from this survey; physical access at the courthouse.
- Church records for denominations other than Congregational (Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Quaker) are largely not in an online index for this county and period; denominational archives must be contacted directly.

## Known record losses

This survey found no tool result stating that specific Berkshire County vital, church, probate, or land records for 1820–1850 were destroyed. The absence of a confirmed loss does not mean every record survives; coverage gaps exist. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts record types (Church Records, Land and Property, Probate, Census, Naming Customs) returned only generic content during this survey — re-run this locality guide before relying on their silence regarding losses.

## Research tips

- **Town is the vital-records unit.** Because Massachusetts recorded births, marriages, and deaths at the town level (not the county level) since 1639, you must know which Berkshire town your family lived in before searching vital records. The county did not consolidate these; each town kept its own series. Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)
- **Use the "Vital Records to 1850" published series first.** For any Berkshire County town, the published transcription volume for that town (available at NEHGS, many public libraries, and potentially on Ancestry) gives the fastest access to births, marriages, and deaths through 1850 without browsing unindexed images. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)
- **Statewide records begin only in 1841.** For 1820–1840 events, statewide indexes do not exist — only town records and church registers cover those years. Do not assume a statewide index covers your whole period.
- **Search across the New York and Vermont lines.** A family in a northern Berkshire town (Adams, Williamstown, Florida) is a short distance from Bennington County, Vermont; a family in a western or southwestern town (Hancock, Richmond, Alford, Egremont, Sheffield) is close to Columbia County, New York. Vital records, deeds, probate, and church records may exist on either side of these borders. The Neighboring Counties table from the Berkshire County wiki page was not available during this survey (the wiki returned only generic content), so the full list of bordering counties should be confirmed directly at the FamilySearch Wiki.
- **NEHGS is the essential regional library.** The New England Historic Genealogical Society in Boston holds compiled genealogies, the "Vital Records to 1850" series, and many Berkshire County-specific collections. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)
- **FamilySearch Wiki unavailable for most Massachusetts topic pages.** During this survey, the FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages (Berkshire County Genealogy home page, Massachusetts getting-started, online-records, and research-tips pages, and all Massachusetts topic pages except Vital Records) returned only generic fallback content. Re-run this locality guide in a fresh session before relying on the absence of anything from those pages.

You are researching a family who lived in Berkshire County, Massachusetts between 1820 and 1850, a county that borders New York and Vermont and where births, marriages, and deaths were recorded town-by-town (not at the county level) under a Massachusetts mandate going back to 1639, with the state beginning to collect copies only in 1841. The most practical first step online is the FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" and the published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series for the specific town; a browse-only FamilySearch image volume (512 images, no index) covers Berkshire County town clerk records through 1850, and a second browse-only volume (274 images) covers Pittsfield's Congregational church, 1791–1850 — for other towns' church records, the individual congregation or its denominational archive must be contacted. Because the town is near both the New York and Vermont lines, vital events, land transactions, and church membership could appear in Bennington County (Vermont) or Columbia County (New York) records as well, so those neighboring jurisdictions should be searched in parallel. The next step is to identify which specific Berkshire town your family lived in, then search that town's entry in the "Vital Records to 1850" published series and the FamilySearch town vital records collection before turning to the unindexed browse volumes.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

> **Survey limitation notice.** The FamilySearch place-resolution tools, collections_search, volume_search, and all Ireland-specific wiki pages (civil registration, land, census, church records, probate, County Antrim genealogy) returned no usable Ireland-specific data during this survey — every Ireland record-type wiki URL resolved to the same generic fallback page. No collection IDs, record counts, or repository details for County Antrim can be grounded in tool output. The one Ireland-specific wiki page that returned substantive content was the **Ireland Naming Customs** page, cited in full below. All other sections represent standard genealogical practice for this jurisdiction and period; each gap is flagged, and FamilySearch Wiki URLs are provided for verification.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish and barony:** Billy is a civil parish within the barony of **Cary**, County Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland.
- **County seat:** Antrim (county town). Billy parish lies in north County Antrim in the Causeway Coast area, near Bushmills.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Province of Ulster. Ireland was administered as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1 January 1801 (Act of Union) through the entire target period.
- **Population figures:** Not returned by any tool for any Irish place during this survey.
- **Economy and denominations:** County Antrim had a strong Ulster Scots Presbyterian character, a linen trade economy, and experienced the United Irish Rebellion of 1798 and the Great Famine (1845–52) — but these details come from background knowledge, not tool output, and are noted here for context only.

---

## Boundary Changes

- Civil parish and barony boundaries in Ireland were defined for the civil registration and census systems introduced in the mid-19th century and are generally treated as stable administrative units for 1780–1870.
- The Local Government (Ireland) Act 1898, which reorganized local government into rural and urban district councils, falls after the target period and does not affect where records from 1780–1870 are held.
- No specific boundary change affecting Billy parish was confirmed by any tool result.

---

## Available Record Types

> **General note:** collections_search and volume_search returned zero results for County Antrim and Ireland. No specific collection titles, IDs, record counts, or digitization levels for any record type below can be grounded in tool output for this survey. Each section gives the FamilySearch Wiki URL to consult for confirmation.

---

### Vital Records — Civil Registration

- **Start date:** Not confirmed by tool output. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Civil_Registration for the registration level and year. (Non-Catholic marriages had an earlier requirement than births and deaths; do not apply a bare date without its registration level.)
- **What exists:** Civil registers of births, marriages, and deaths are the primary target for events from the mid-19th century onward.
- **Where held:** PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Belfast) and the General Register Office are the established custodians for County Antrim civil records — but specific holdings and access were not returned by any tool.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers are the primary source for events before civil registration began.

---

### Church Records

- **Denominations present in County Antrim during this period:** Church of Ireland, Presbyterian (dominant in many north Antrim areas), Roman Catholic, Methodist. Which congregations specifically served Billy parish was not confirmed by any tool.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Presbyterian session records and communicants' rolls.
- **Where held:** PRONI holds microfilm copies of many County Antrim church registers; the Representative Church Body Library (Dublin) holds Church of Ireland originals not at PRONI; the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland holds many Presbyterian registers. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- **Language:** Church of Ireland and Presbyterian registers in County Antrim were kept in English throughout the target period. Roman Catholic registers may also be in English; check each register.
- **Gaps for Billy parish:** No specific destroyed or missing registers were confirmed by any tool.

---

### Census Records

- **Irish national censuses during the period:** 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871 — but survival and availability for County Antrim were not confirmed by tool output. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Census
- **Census substitutes:** Land valuation records (Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Primary Valuation) serve as the primary census substitute for heads of household before or alongside civil registration. No specific substitute census for Billy parish was confirmed by tool output.
- **Known census losses:** Most pre-1901 Irish census returns were destroyed (1922 Four Courts fire and earlier deliberate destruction); this is contextual background, not a confirmed tool result.

---

### Land Records

- **Survey system:** Ireland used townlands and baronies rather than a rectangular survey. County Antrim falls within this structure.
- **Key record classes for 1780–1870:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books** (c. 1823–1837): lists taxable landholders, widely used as a census substitute.
  - **Griffith's Primary Valuation** (surveyed county by county in the 1840s–1860s): lists all occupiers of land and property, the most important mid-century household census substitute.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by tool output. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property
- **Note:** Specific availability for Billy parish was not returned by any tool.

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianship records.
- **Where held:** PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland (Dublin) are established repositories for pre-partition Irish probate records. Specific County Antrim holdings were not returned by any tool. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** 1798 Rebellion, Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815), Crimean War (1853–1856).
- **Record types:** British Army service records, pension records, muster rolls.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (UK, Kew) holds British Army records; PRONI holds some Ulster militia and yeomanry records. Specific holdings not confirmed by tool output. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Military_Records

---

### Cemetery Records

Obituaries, marriage notices, land sale notices, and legal notices are the most genealogically valuable content for this period.

### Immigration and Emigration Records

- **Context:** County Antrim experienced significant emigration, especially during and after the Great Famine (1845–1852), to North America and Australia.
- **Relevant departure ports:** Belfast, Londonderry, and Liverpool.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization papers, and alien registrations — created in the destination country, not Ireland. NARA (United States) and Library and Archives Canada hold passenger lists for the main destinations; Belfast emigration manifests exist for the port itself.
- **Research tip:** Examine the full passenger manifest page, not just the index entry — infants and children traveling with parents appear on the same manifest image.

---

### Tax Records

- **Types:** Hearth money rolls (earlier period); county cess/grand jury presentments; Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837).
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by tool output. Consult: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property for tithe records and PRONI for county tax series.
- **Substitute value:** Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation together serve as the primary census substitute for the decades before civil registration.

---

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|

| **National Archives of Ireland**, Dublin | Pre-partition probate, census, land, and state records | In-person / online catalogue |
| **Representative Church Body Library**, Dublin | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland**, Belfast | Presbyterian session records and registers | In-person |

> Note: These are established custodians for Irish records as a class. Specific holdings for Billy parish were not confirmed by any tool result during this survey. Verify holdings before visiting or ordering records.

### Online Starting Points (Unconfirmed by Tool — for Verification)

- FamilySearch Wiki — County Antrim: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim,_Ireland_Genealogy
- Ireland Civil Registration: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Civil_Registration
- Ireland Church Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records
- Ireland Census: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Census
- Ireland Land and Property: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property
- Ireland Probate Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records
- Ireland Military Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Military_Records

---

## Naming Conventions

> **Source:** The following points come directly from the **FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Naming Customs** page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs), the one Ireland-specific wiki page that returned substantive content during this survey. Every point here is based on that confirmed tool result.

- Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were commonly anglicized under English rule, producing many variant forms. A family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn in the same parish register across different decades.
- The prefixes **Mac** (son of) and **O** (grandson/descendant of) were frequently dropped or restored over time. Search all variants — with prefix, without prefix, and with alternate spellings.
- Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may appear in several forms within one parish register.
- Given names were also anglicized from Gaelic originals. For example, Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah are all recorded variants of the same underlying name.
- Some given names were used for both males and females — Florence, Sydney, and Evelyn among them.
- A **traditional naming pattern** was often followed until the later 19th century:
  - 1st son → father's father
  - 2nd son → mother's father
  - 3rd son → father
  - 4th son → father's eldest brother
  - 1st daughter → mother's mother
  - 2nd daughter → father's mother
  - 3rd daughter → mother
  
  This pattern is a research clue, not a rule. It was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start at PRONI.** PRONI in Belfast is the primary repository for County Antrim church registers, land records, and estate papers. Its online catalogue can be searched by parish name before visiting. Identify which denominations served Billy parish and confirm whether their registers survive and from what year.

2. **Check the townland.** Billy civil parish contains multiple townlands. All Irish land and census records are indexed at the townland level; knowing the specific townland(s) where your family lived narrows searches considerably. Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books are both townland-organized.

3. **A negative online result is not absence.** Because no digitized collections for County Antrim were confirmed during this survey, an empty FamilySearch or Ancestry search does not mean records do not exist — they may be undigitized, unindexed, or held only at PRONI or a denominational archive.

4. **Survey adjoining County Londonderry.** Billy parish lies near the County Londonderry (Derry) boundary. Families near that border likely generated records on both sides. Check Presbyterian and Church of Ireland registers that may cross the county line.

5. **Re-run this guide.** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ireland civil registration, land, census, church records, probate, and County Antrim all resolved to generic content during this survey. Re-running the guide when the wiki-query tools are fully operational — or consulting those pages directly — is essential before planning searches.

---

*This guide was produced with the Ireland Naming Customs FamilySearch Wiki page as the only confirmed Ireland-specific tool result. All record-type descriptions reflect standard genealogical practice for this jurisdiction and period. Verify all repository holdings and collection availability before planning searches.*

- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by tool output from the Ireland Land and Property wiki page (which returned only generic content during this survey). Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property.
- **Types:** The two most important land record classes for the target period are the Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837) and Griffith's Primary Valuation (surveyed county by county in the 1840s–1860s). These are widely cited as the primary census substitutes for pre-civil-registration Ireland, but their specific availability for Billy parish was not confirmed by tool output during this survey.
- **Date range and where held:** Not confirmed by tool output.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The period 1780–1870 encompasses the American Revolutionary War, the United Irish Rebellion of 1798, the Napoleonic Wars, and the Crimean War (1853–1856).
- **Record types:** British Army service records, pension records, and muster rolls are the primary classes for men from County Antrim serving in this period.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by tool output. The National Archives (UK, Kew) holds British Army records; PRONI holds some Ulster-related militia and yeomanry records. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Military_Records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by tool output for Billy parish.
- **Online coverage:** No Ireland-specific cemetery index URLs were returned by external_links_search (which returned only generic US-focused links).
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and vestry burial registers, where they survive, are held at the relevant church or at PRONI. Not confirmed by tool output for Billy parish.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Not confirmed by tool output for County Antrim or north Antrim specifically.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by tool output. The British Newspaper Archive and the National Library of Ireland are established holders of Irish historical newspapers but were not returned by any tool during this survey.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, land sale notices, and legal notices are valuable for the target period.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** County Antrim experienced significant emigration, particularly during and after the Great Famine (1845–1852), to North America and elsewhere.
- **Relevant ports:** Emigrants from north Antrim typically left through Belfast, Londonderry, or directly via Liverpool. Arrival records in the United States, Canada, and Australia are therefore relevant complement sources.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization papers, and alien registrations are the primary classes for emigrants. Inland declarations of intention and naturalization records were created in the destination country, not in Ireland.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by tool output. NARA (United States) and Library and Archives Canada hold passenger lists for the main destination countries; Belfast had its own emigration manifests. The tools returned no specific URLs or collections.
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching an emigrating family from Billy parish, examine the full manifest page for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Hearth money rolls and later county cess/grand jury presentments; the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) function as a household census substitute.
- **Date range and where held:** Not confirmed by tool output. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property for tithe records and PRONI for county tax series.
- **Substitute value:** Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation together serve as the primary census substitute for the decades before civil registration in Ireland.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch Wiki — County Antrim | No collections confirmed by tool during this survey | Starting point for all record types | Free (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim,_Ireland_Genealogy) |

No Ireland-specific repository URLs were returned by external_links_search, collections_search, or volume_search. The 6 links returned by external_links_search were generic US-focused resources (US census, NARA, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, Ancestry US census) with no relevance to County Antrim, Ireland. They are not listed in this table as Ireland resources.

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search and collections_search both returned zero results for County Antrim and Ireland. No digitized volumes or indexed collections could be identified from tool output for this place and period.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| PRONI — Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Belfast | Church register microfilms, land records, census fragments — not confirmed in detail by tool | In-person / online catalogue (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni) |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Pre-partition probate, census, land, and state records — not confirmed in detail by tool | In-person / online catalogue |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records — not confirmed in detail by tool | In-person |
| Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, Belfast | Presbyterian session and register records — not confirmed in detail by tool | In-person |

Note: the repositories listed above are established custodians for Irish records as a class; their specific holdings for Billy parish were not stated by any tool result during this survey. Verify holdings before visiting.

## Records NOT online

This survey cannot classify any record type as online or not online, because collections_search and volume_search returned zero results for County Antrim and Ireland. No digitization levels can be stated from tool output.

## Known record losses

No tool result during this survey stated a specific record loss for Billy parish or County Antrim. The widespread destruction of Irish census records (most pre-1901 returns) and the Four Courts fire of 1922 (which destroyed many original pre-partition records) are contextually significant but were not returned by any tool result in this run and therefore cannot be cited as confirmed findings of this guide.

## Research tips

- **Naming conventions — from the Ireland Naming Customs page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs), which returned specific content and is the basis for every point in this section only:**
  - Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were commonly anglicized under English rule, producing many variant forms. A family may appear as O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn in the same parish register across different decades.
  - The prefixes Mac (son of) and O (grandson or descendant of) were frequently dropped or restored over time, so search all variants — with prefix, without prefix, and with alternate spellings.
  - Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded in several different ways within one parish.
  - Given names were also anglicized from Gaelic originals: Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah are all variations of the same underlying name, per the FamilySearch Wiki.
  - Some given names are used for both males and females — Florence, Sydney, and Evelyn among them.
  - A traditional naming pattern was often followed until the later 19th century: the first son was usually named for the father's father; the second son for the mother's father; the third son for the father; the fourth son for the father's eldest brother; the first daughter for the mother's mother; the second daughter for the father's mother; the third daughter for the mother. This pattern is a clue, not a rule — it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.
- **Re-run this guide.** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ireland civil registration, land records, census, church records, probate, and County Antrim returned only generic redirected content during this survey. Re-running the locality guide when the wiki-query-api is fully operational, or consulting the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Antrim,_Ireland_Genealogy, is essential before planning searches.
- **A negative online result is not absence.** Because no digitized collections or volumes were confirmed for County Antrim in this survey, an empty FamilySearch or Ancestry search does not mean records do not exist — they may be undigitized, unindexed, or held only at PRONI or a denominational archive.
- **Survey adjoining counties.** Billy parish lies in north County Antrim near the boundary with County Londonderry (Derry). Families near that border likely generated records on both sides. The adjoining counties were not listed by any tool result (the County Antrim wiki page did not return), so check County Londonderry sources as well, particularly for Presbyterian and Church of Ireland registers that may cross the county line.

---

This guide was built without reliable output from the FamilySearch Wiki (all Ireland-specific record-type pages returned generic redirected content) and without any results from the place-resolution or collection-search tools. The one confirmed source is the Ireland Naming Customs page from the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs), which grounds the naming conventions section in full.

---

The records for Billy civil parish in County Antrim survive primarily in church registers (Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, and Roman Catholic) held at PRONI in Belfast, supplemented by land valuation records such as the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation for the decades before civil registration began, and the county's civil birth, marriage, and death registers from the mid-19th century onward — but during this survey the research tools could not reach the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ireland or resolve Irish place names, so none of those specific collections or repositories could be confirmed from tool output, and the guide should be re-run with working tools before searches are planned. The most important immediate step for research in this parish is to consult the FamilySearch Wiki's County Antrim genealogy page and PRONI's online catalogue directly to identify which church registers survive for Billy parish, then work outward from there into land and civil records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from parts of Berks and Northampton Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the survey tools for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated the county throughout this period; iron manufacturing and railroading supplemented it.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish and Welsh immigration tied to coal mining; German settlers also present, reflected in German-language church records.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic, Methodist, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Welsh Calvinist, Presbyterian, and others.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid population growth from anthracite coal expansion; Civil War (1861–1865) produced military service, pension, and draft records.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from parts of Berks and Northampton Counties.
- Boundaries within the target period (1840–1880) were stable.
- Records for events before 1811 are under Berks or Northampton County, depending on where within the later county the event occurred; search both predecessors unless location is known precisely.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for the Pennsylvania Vital Records page and did not state registration dates. No civil birth or death collections covering 1840–1880 were returned; the earliest death certificate collection found is Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (collection 2255317), beginning in 1906. Marriage collections covering the period are available.
- **What exists:** Marriage records: a browse-only digitized volume of Schuylkill County Marriage Records 1870–1910 (image group 007936753, 94 images, 0% indexed); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, 156,023 images); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images — index/compiled only). No birth or death civil registration collections for 1840–1880 were found.
- **Where held:** County-level marriages: Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville; FamilySearch digitized images at familysearch.org.
- **Gaps:** No indexed civil birth or death records for 1840–1880. Marriage Records volume (007936753) is browse-only and must be examined image by image.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials, marriages); cemetery records; probate records; newspaper death and marriage notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic, Methodist, German Lutheran, German Reformed, Welsh Calvinist, Presbyterian, and others served the coal-mining population. German-language records present.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Schuylkill County Church Records (image group 007936751, 187 images, 1842–1895) in English and German; it is browse-only (0% name-indexed) and must be examined image by image. German-language literacy is required for German sections. FamilySearch also lists 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, labeled 'synthetic test fixture,' 1708–1985, 1,245,830 records) — verify its real-collection status before relying on it.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content and did not name which Schuylkill County congregations' registers survive or their archival locations.
- **Language:** English and German.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Federal census enumerations for 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 cover Schuylkill County.
