- **Start date:** Per [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records), statewide civil registration of births and deaths was not required until 1906 (state level). Philadelphia County began local registration in 1860 (local/county level); Allegheny County in 1870 (local/county level). Marriage licenses were kept at the county courthouse from the colonial period.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records (licenses and bonds) from the colonial period. No birth or death civil records exist for the late 1700s at any statewide level.
- **Where held:** County courthouse for marriage records; FamilySearch collection 1571957 (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950) and collection 1502909 (Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900)
- **Gaps:** No statewide births or deaths in this period — Quaker meeting registers and other church records are the primary vital record substitutes
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker monthly meeting birth, marriage, and death registers; German Reformed and Lutheran baptismal registers; family Bibles; county newspaper notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Society of Friends (Quakers) — predominant in Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia counties; German Reformed and Lutheran — common throughout eastern Pennsylvania; Anglican/Episcopal — Philadelphia and larger towns; Presbyterian — widespread; Mennonite and Amish — Lancaster and surrounding counties; Catholic — Philadelphia
- **Record types:** Quaker monthly meetings recorded births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers when members moved to another meeting), and disciplinary proceedings (disownments). Per [Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), Quaker marriage certificates were signed by all witnesses present, making them an unusually detailed genealogical source. Other denominations recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **Where held:** The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College (Swarthmore, Pennsylvania) holds the largest collection of American Quaker records, per [Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records). FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers. One digitized volume is available on FamilySearch: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images) — it is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and must be browsed image by image with no name search.
- **Gaps:** Most individual monthly meeting registers have not been digitized and are available only on microfilm at FamilySearch or in the original at the Friends Historical Library
- **Published abstracts:** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states, per [Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts). This indexed work is a practical first step before seeking the original registers.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census (1790) covered Pennsylvania; it lists free white males by age group, free white females, all other free persons, and slaves by count only. No federal census predates 1790.
- **State/provincial census:** No Pennsylvania state census for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists (tax duplicates) survive from the 1690s in some counties and are the primary census substitute before 1790. Per [Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), the 1693 Chester County tax list is one of the earliest surviving colonial tax records.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed. Tax lists are largely not indexed online and are held at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (testate estates), letters of administration (intestate), inventories, guardianships, letters testamentary
- **Date range:** From the colonial period; FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) covers this range
- **Where held:** County Register of Wills at the county courthouse. Collection 1999196 contains 3,200,560 images but has 0 indexed records — it is browse-only and must be searched image by image.
- **Note:** Quaker religious practice did not exempt members from civil probate. Quaker estates generated the same county probate records as any other resident.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds — Pennsylvania was a proprietary colony, not a public-domain land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Per [Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records), land records begin with William Penn's original grants (1681). The Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records covering the colonial and early national periods.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, county deed books, mortgages
- **Date range:** Land Office records from 1681; county deed books from each county's formation date
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives / Land Office (Harrisburg) for original grants; county Recorder of Deeds for deed books

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA); Pennsylvania state pension records; bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal pension and service records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state-level militia records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records
- **Quaker note:** Quakers were pacifists; many refused military service and were disowned by their meeting for bearing arms. Disciplinary minutes of monthly meetings may note members who took up arms — itself a genealogical finding. After disownment, switch to civil records for continued coverage.

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Quaker meetings maintained their own burial grounds adjacent to meetinghouses, often minimally marked. Burial records, when they survive, are part of the monthly meeting's register.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers some Pennsylvania Quaker burial grounds; coverage for the late 1700s is incomplete.
- **Physical records:** Monthly meeting burial registers are held at the Friends Historical Library or on FamilySearch microfilm

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Pennsylvania Gazette (Philadelphia, founded 1728) is the most prominent paper of this period; it carried obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices
- **Where held:** Digitized on Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for some titles; Library of Congress and American Antiquarian Society hold additional holdings
- **Content value:** Marriage notices and death notices in Philadelphia-area papers may supplement missing vital records for the late 1700s

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the dominant port of entry for this region throughout the colonial and early national periods
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (Philadelphia port records); naturalization records filed at county courts
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists; pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Quaker removal certificates:** When a Quaker moved from one monthly meeting to another, they carried a certificate of removal signed by the home meeting and filed it at the receiving meeting. These documents trace migration between communities and function as an internal immigration/emigration record unique to the Quaker world.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Assessment lists (tax duplicates), property tax, poll tax
- **Date range:** From the 1690s in some counties
- **Where held:** County archives and Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax assessment lists are the primary census substitute before the 1790 federal census; they can establish residence and approximate wealth across consecutive years

### Other record types
- **Quaker disownment records:** Members who married outside the meeting, bore arms, or violated other conduct rules were formally disowned; minutes record the name, offense, and date, and sometimes note reinstatement. These are found in monthly meeting minutes at the Friends Historical Library or on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Quaker removal certificates:** Certificates of transfer between meetings name the person, their destination, and often family members — the Quaker equivalent of a change-of-address record. Search both the sending meeting (which issued it) and the receiving meeting (which should have recorded receipt).
- **School records:** Quakers were early founders of schools in Pennsylvania; some early school registers survive at the Friends Historical Library.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909); Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, browse-only images); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, browse-only) | Marriage records and probate from the colonial period; Quaker minutes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | 1790 federal census for Pennsylvania | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Revolutionary War pension and service records; Philadelphia passenger lists | Free/In-person |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Quaker burial grounds | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Marriage notices and death notices before civil registration | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches the Religious record type for Pennsylvania in the 1750–1810 period: Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 (image group 001188322, 145 images, browse-only). This was the complete result set — no additional pages exist. Additional volumes may exist under record-type filters not searched in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College | Largest U.S. collection of Quaker records: monthly meeting minutes, birth/marriage/death registers, removal certificates, disciplinary minutes | In-person or written inquiry; swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Land Office records (warrants, surveys, patents), county tax lists, state militia records | In-person; phmc.pa.gov |
| County courthouses (Register of Wills; Recorder of Deeds) | Probate records, deed books, marriage licenses — from each county's formation date | In-person or mail |
| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilm of Quaker monthly meeting registers, Pennsylvania county records | In-person; microfilm available on loan at FamilySearch centers |

## Records NOT online
- Most Quaker monthly meeting birth, marriage, and death registers — available on FamilySearch microfilm or at the Friends Historical Library; search FamilySearch.org catalog by meeting name for specific microfilm numbers
- Pennsylvania tax assessment lists (pre-1790) — held at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives; not comprehensively indexed online
- County probate record indexes for the colonial period — collection 1999196 has 3.2 million images but no name index; must be browsed
- County deed books — not comprehensively digitized or indexed online for the late 1700s
- Removal certificates and disownment minutes beyond the one digitized volume listed above

## Known record losses
No tool result returned in this survey identified specific destroyed or lost record classes for Pennsylvania in the late 1700s. The absence of statewide vital registration before 1906 is a legislative gap, not a record loss — such records were never created at the state level. For specific counties, consult the Pennsylvania State Archives or the county courthouse to determine whether a particular series survived.

## Research tips
- **Start with the meeting, not the county.** Each Quaker monthly meeting kept its own records, and those follow the meeting's geographic jurisdiction, not county lines. Identify which monthly meeting served the community where your ancestors lived. Use Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* to find abstracts before seeking the original register at Swarthmore or on FamilySearch microfilm ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)).
- **Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia counties first.** These counties had the densest Quaker populations in the colonial and early national periods ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)). If you do not know exactly where in Pennsylvania the ancestor lived, begin here.
- **Use removal certificates to trace migration.** When an ancestor disappears from one meeting's records, search for a removal certificate in both the sending meeting (which issued it) and the receiving meeting (which recorded its receipt). This is the Quaker equivalent of a forwarding address.
- **Tax lists before 1790.** Because there is no Pennsylvania census before 1790, county tax assessment lists from the 1690s onward establish residence and can be read across consecutive years to track family members ([Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)).
- **Disownment does not mean disappearance.** A Quaker disowned for marrying outside the meeting or bearing arms often remained in the same community. After disownment, switch to civil records (deed, probate, tax) for continued coverage — the meeting records will stop.
- **Marriage certificates list all witnesses.** Quaker marriage certificates were signed by everyone present at the wedding. A surviving certificate may name dozens of family members and neighbors who appear in no other record — look for the original certificate in the monthly meeting's marriage register, not just an abstract ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)).

Here is the locality guide produced for Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (c. 1860–1910):

---

## Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Era Locality Guide

### Key Context

- **Vital registration gaps:** Civil birth and death registration in Allegheny County did not begin until 1870, and statewide registration only started in 1906. For most of the steel boom era, **church baptism and burial registers are the primary source of vital events**, not government certificates.
- **Allegheny City:** Anyone living on what is now Pittsburgh's North Side before 1907 would appear in records under **"Allegheny city"** — a separate municipality until it was annexed by Pittsburgh that year.

---

### Occupational & Industrial Sources

| Source | Held at / Access |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Pittsburgh city directories** (listing occupation and address, 1813 onward, issued annually) | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh |
| **Company employment records** (fragmentary) | Senator John Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives |
| **Federal census occupation columns** (1870, 1880, 1900, 1910) | FamilySearch, Ancestry |

City directories are the highest-yield first step — they anchor a subject year-by-year with occupation and address before census years.

---

### Vital & Church Records

- **Ethnic Catholic parishes** are critical for immigrant steelworkers. Each nationality (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) maintained **separate registers**. Originals are mostly held physically at the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**.
- Protestant and other denominational records vary widely by congregation.

---

### Naturalization Records

- **Allegheny County naturalizations (1798–1930)** are at the **National Archives, Philadelphia region**.
- These often name the immigrant's **specific place of origin** — the key to opening research in the home country.

---

### Census Records

- The **1880 census** is the most complete for the core steel era and includes birthplace of parents.
- The **1900 census** adds immigration year and years in the United States.

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **City directories** (Carnegie Library) — anchor the subject by year, confirm occupation and address
2. **1880 and 1900 federal censuses** — family data, immigration year, parents' birthplaces
3. **Naturalization records** (NARA Philadelphia) — country and region of origin
4. **Ethnic parish registers** (Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives) — baptism, marriage, burial
5. **Company/employment records** (Heinz History Center, Rivers of Steel) — industrial corroboration

---

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Allegheny County at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) is worth consulting directly for additional collection listings. entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No indexed population data was returned by tools; Pittsburgh was among the largest U.S. cities by 1900, with Allegheny County's population driven by the steel boom
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing dominated from the 1870s onward; Carnegie Steel and related firms made Pittsburgh the center of American steel production, attracting massive immigrant labor flows (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh)
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrants poured into the city and surrounding mill towns during the late 1800s
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (with numerous ethnic parishes organized by nationality), mainline Protestant; ethnic Catholic parishes were the primary record-keeping institutions for many immigrant families
- **Key historical events:** Steel industry boom of the 1870s–1900s drove massive immigration; the Homestead Strike (1892) is a notable event affecting labor records

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County has been stable since its formation in 1788.
- The city of Allegheny (across the Ohio and Allegheny rivers from Pittsburgh) was a separate municipality until annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. - **Match the ethnic background to the right Catholic parish.** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and Irish parishes each maintained separate registers; using the wrong parish will produce a dead end. Identify the specific ethnic parish (often indicated by the census or city directory neighborhood), then contact the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))
- **Naturalization records document arrival and birthplace.** Pre-1906 naturalizations at the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930) are at the National Archives at Philadelphia — these often state the immigrant's county and country of origin, which unlocks foreign research. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))
- **Vital records before 1906 were NOT statewide in Pennsylvania.** For births and deaths in the late 1800s, search both Allegheny County records (from 1870) and church registers; do not assume the statewide death certificate system covers these years. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages returned only generic content during this survey.** The Allegheny County page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy and the Pennsylvania pages should be checked directly — they may carry additional detail not captured here.

Here is the locality guide produced for Philadelphia during the 1793 yellow fever epidemic (saved as **loc_001** in your project):

---

## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Research Guide

**Coverage period:** ca. 1780–1810, centered on the 1793 epidemic.

### The Core Research Challenge
Pennsylvania had **no civil registration in 1793**, so there is no central death register. Research depends on a combination of church records and epidemic-specific sources.

---

### Key Record Types and Repositories

#### 1. Church Burial Registers *(most important source)*
Because deaths were recorded by congregations, not the state, the church registers are the primary finding tool for epidemic deaths:
- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) — one of Philadelphia's largest congregations; its burial registers survive and cover this period.
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church** — the oldest church in Pennsylvania; burial records survive.
- **Other Philadelphia congregations** — Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, and Quaker meeting records; each maintained its own registers.

Many of these have been microfilmed. Check the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** and the **Presbyterian Historical Society** for holdings.

---

#### 2. Epidemic-Specific Sources *(unique to the 1793 outbreak)*

Three sources name individuals who died or received aid during the epidemic:

| Source | Description | Repository |
|--------|-------------|------------|
| **Mathew Carey's published account** (*A Short Account of the Malignant Fever*, 1793) | Names the dead and details the epidemic; multiple editions exist | HSP, Philadelphia City Archives, digitized copies online |
| **Committee of Citizens minutes** | The citizen relief committee kept records of those assisted | Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Bush Hill Hospital records** | The epidemic hospital's patient records | Philadelphia City Archives |

---

#### 3. Federal Census Records *(bracket the epidemic)*
- **1790 U.S. Federal Census** — identifies households *before* the epidemic; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **1800 U.S. Federal Census** — identifies surviving households *after* the epidemic; absence of a head of household may indicate death in 1793

---

#### 4. Probate and Estate Records
Deaths in 1793 generated a surge of estate filings. Wills and administrations from this period are held at:
- **Philadelphia Register of Wills** / **Philadelphia City Archives**
- Indexed records may be available through FamilySearch

---

#### 5. Newspaper Death Notices
Philadelphia newspapers published lengthy lists of epidemic deaths. Key papers:
- *Federal Gazette*
- *Philadelphia Gazette*
- *General Advertiser*

Holdings are at HSP and the **Library Company of Philadelphia**; some have been digitized through Chronicling America or Accessible Archives.

---

### Primary Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|------------|---------------|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Church registers, Carey's account, manuscript collections, newspapers |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Committee minutes, Bush Hill records, municipal records |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Printed sources, newspapers, Carey's pamphlet |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society** | Presbyterian congregation records |
| **FamilySearch** | Microfilmed church records, census, probate indexes |

---

### Important Caveat
The FamilySearch Research Wiki was unreachable during this survey, so specific FamilySearch collection IDs and wiki guidance could not be confirmed. Before relying on this guide, verify against [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy](https://familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy) to catch any gaps.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Search the 1790 and 1800 censuses** to identify your family before and after the epidemic.
2. **Contact HSP and the Philadelphia City Archives** (both offer online inquiry services) to establish whether the epidemic-specific records and your family's church registers have been digitized.
3. **Search Mathew Carey's published account** — it is widely available and names many of the dead by name.
4. **Identify the family's congregation** to target the right church burial register.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the city of Philadelphia incorporated within it
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making it the largest city in the United States at the time; roughly 5,000 died in the 1793 epidemic (Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793)
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; mercantile, shipping, and artisan trades dominant
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English, German, Scots-Irish, with significant Quaker, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, and Catholic communities
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, German Reformed, and others
- **Key historical events:** The yellow fever epidemic of August–November 1793 killed approximately 5,000 people (one-tenth of the population) and caused thousands more to flee; this is the defining event for genealogical research in this period

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County and City boundaries were essentially coterminous for this period; no significant boundary changes affected the jurisdiction between 1780 and 1810.
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 later unified city and county, but that is outside the target window.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates" (collection 1255317) begins in 1906, confirming statewide registration began at the state level around that date. The wiki_search result states: "church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906" (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil death, birth, or marriage certificates. Church registers and special epidemic documentation substitute entirely.
- **Where held:** No civil vital registration records exist for 1793 Philadelphia.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; Mathew Carey's published list of the dead; Committee records; church marriage registers.

### Epidemic-specific records (1793)
These are the primary finding tools for the yellow fever period and have no equivalent in ordinary years:
- **Mathew Carey's account:** A published list of names of the dead compiled during and shortly after the epidemic. Held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Committee of Citizens records:** Minutes and reports of the citizen committee organized to respond to the epidemic document individuals aided, deceased, or relocated. Held at Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the emergency hospital that treated epidemic patients. Held at Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Access:** These are physical records at their holding repositories; digitization status was not confirmed by any tool in this survey.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, one of the most complete registers), Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes', founded 1642), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Parish archives, denominational archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (indexes), and FamilySearch microfilm. FamilySearch has digitized one volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800), image group 001188322, covering 145 images; it is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and must be browsed image by image.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki was unreachable during this survey, so a complete list of surviving registers cannot be confirmed from tool results. The wiki_search result names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') as among the most complete for the epidemic period.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') registers may include Swedish or German passages in earlier volumes.
- **Note:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records); consult their published indexes before searching raw registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the closest enumeration before the epidemic and would show pre-epidemic household composition. The 1800 census shows survivors and family reconstitution after the epidemic. Both are name-indexed and available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania had no regular state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia tax records (see Tax records below) function as a quasi-census for property owners.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships (for orphaned children of epidemic victims)
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) covers this period; it holds 3,200,560 images but is browse-only (no index, no full-text search) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Register of Wills and Orphans' Court, Philadelphia City Archives. The 1793–1794 period saw a surge in probate filings due to epidemic deaths; the Orphans' Court records are especially important for identifying minor children left without parents.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images on FamilySearch (collection 1999196); physical originals at Philadelphia City Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Proprietary land grants under the Penn family; deed recording at the county level. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property were unreachable during this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (common in Philadelphia), tax records
- **Date range:** Deed books from colonial period through this window
- **Where held:** Recorder of Deeds, Philadelphia City Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) produced service records and pension files for veterans still living in Philadelphia in 1793. The War of 1812 (1812–1815) is at the edge of the target window.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA (Fold3: https://www.fold3.com/; NARA: https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Mikveh Israel Cemetery (Jewish), and multiple other church burial grounds throughout the city. Epidemic burials in 1793 were sometimes in ad hoc locations outside normal church grounds due to the volume of deaths.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed headstone data for some Philadelphia cemeteries; coverage for 1793 is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches and their archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793, including the Pennsylvania Gazette and Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser. These carried death notices, estate notices, and legal announcements during and after the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized holdings; Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania for physical copies and microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, legal notices, and contemporary epidemic accounts naming individuals

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was a major Atlantic port of entry; passenger arrival records are relevant for newly arrived families.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (pre-1820 lists are sparse); naturalization petitions filed in Philadelphia courts
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, 1700–1900) may assist with immigrant family identification.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, with focus on the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the city of Philadelphia incorporated within it
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making it the largest city in the United States at the time; roughly 5,000 died in the 1793 epidemic (Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793)
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port; mercantile, shipping, and artisan trades dominant
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English, German, Scots-Irish, with significant Quaker, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, and Catholic communities
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, German Reformed, and others
- **Key historical events:** The yellow fever epidemic of August–November 1793 killed approximately 5,000 people (one-tenth of the population) and caused thousands more to flee; this is the defining event for genealogical research in this period

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County and City boundaries were essentially coterminous for this period; no significant boundary changes affected the jurisdiction between 1780 and 1810.
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 later unified city and county, but that is outside the target window.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates" (collection 1255317) begins in 1906, confirming statewide registration began at the state level around that date. The wiki_search result states: "church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906" (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil death, birth, or marriage certificates. Church registers and special epidemic documentation substitute entirely.
- **Where held:** No civil vital registration records exist for 1793 Philadelphia.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; Mathew Carey's published list of the dead; Committee records; church marriage registers.

### Epidemic-specific records (1793)
These are the primary finding tools for the yellow fever period and have no equivalent in ordinary years:
- **Mathew Carey's account:** A published list of names of the dead compiled during and shortly after the epidemic. Held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Committee of Citizens records:** Minutes and reports of the citizen committee organized to respond to the epidemic document individuals aided, deceased, or relocated. Held at Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Records of the emergency hospital that treated epidemic patients. Held at Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Access:** These are physical records at their holding repositories; digitization status was not confirmed by any tool in this survey.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, one of the most complete registers), Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes', founded 1642), Quaker (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Parish archives, denominational archives, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (indexes), and FamilySearch microfilm. FamilySearch has digitized one volume of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800), image group 001188322, covering 145 images; it is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and must be browsed image by image.
- **Gaps:** The FamilySearch Wiki was unreachable during this survey, so a complete list of surviving registers cannot be confirmed from tool results. The wiki_search result names Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') as among the most complete for the epidemic period.
- **Language:** Most records are in English; Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') registers may include Swedish or German passages in earlier volumes.
- **Note:** The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records); consult their published indexes before searching raw registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census is the closest enumeration before the epidemic and would show pre-epidemic household composition. The 1800 census shows survivors and family reconstitution after the epidemic. Both are name-indexed and available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania had no regular state census in this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia tax records (see Tax records below) function as a quasi-census for property owners.
- **Access:** 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed and online.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships (for orphaned children of epidemic victims)
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196) covers this period; it holds 3,200,560 images but is browse-only (no index, no full-text search) — must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Register of Wills and Orphans' Court, Philadelphia City Archives. The 1793–1794 period saw a surge in probate filings due to epidemic deaths; the Orphans' Court records are especially important for identifying minor children left without parents.
- **Access level:** Browse-only images on FamilySearch (collection 1999196); physical originals at Philadelphia City Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania was not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Proprietary land grants under the Penn family; deed recording at the county level. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Land and Property were unreachable during this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (common in Philadelphia), tax records
- **Date range:** Deed books from colonial period through this window
- **Where held:** Recorder of Deeds, Philadelphia City Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) produced service records and pension files for veterans still living in Philadelphia in 1793. The War of 1812 (1812–1815) is at the edge of the target window.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files at NARA (Fold3: https://www.fold3.com/; NARA: https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration for federal records; Pennsylvania State Archives for state records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard, Mikveh Israel Cemetery (Jewish), and multiple other church burial grounds throughout the city. Epidemic burials in 1793 were sometimes in ad hoc locations outside normal church grounds due to the volume of deaths.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) holds transcribed headstone data for some Philadelphia cemeteries; coverage for 1793 is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual churches and their archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793, including the Pennsylvania Gazette and Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser. These carried death notices, estate notices, and legal announcements during and after the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized holdings; Philadelphia City Archives and Historical Society of Pennsylvania for physical copies and microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, legal notices, and contemporary epidemic accounts naming individuals

## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871: Records & Repositories

### The Core Challenge
The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and with it most pre-1871 civil records — deeds, probate files, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers. | Source | Why It Survived | Where to Find It |
|---|---|---|

| **Chicago Title & Trust Co. insurance records** | Pre-fire property evidence | Chicago History Museum (not online) |
| **Church registers outside the burn zone** | Some parishes were spared | Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives |

| Cook County Births | ~1.45 million | 1871–1940 |

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (ca. 1850–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (statehood 1818)
- **Population during period:** Population figures could not be confirmed by the place_population tool for this survey.
- **Economy:** Meatpacking, rail hub, lumber, manufacturing, commerce — a rapidly growing immigrant industrial city
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Scandinavian, and Eastern European immigrant communities by the 1870s; the fire's displacement exacerbated record gaps for these groups
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish congregations, and many others reflecting the city's immigrant population
- **Key historical events:** Great Fire of October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, displaced more than 100,000 residents, and wiped out most pre-1871 civil and many church records (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during the 1850–1900 period; Chicago's city limits expanded through annexation but records remained at the county level
- No parent-jurisdiction succession issues for this period

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and no specific registration start dates could be confirmed from it. The FamilySearch collections for Cook County begin in 1871 for births (collection 2024189), deaths (collection 1913456), and marriages (collection 1756321) — consistent with the destruction of pre-fire records.
- **What exists:** Birth certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records, collection 2024189); death records 1871–1947 (980,000 records, collection 1913456); marriage records 1871–1920 (620,000 records, collection 1756321) — all on FamilySearch
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office holds originals; FamilySearch has indexed digital collections
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 civil vital records were largely destroyed in the Great Fire; statewide Illinois registration dates were not confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, city directories, federal census, newspaper notices, insurance records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Episcopal, Jewish, and many ethnic-community churches; FamilySearch collection 1803978 covers Cook County Chicago church records 1833–1925 (285,000 records)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Catholic records at the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives; other denominations at their respective archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire registers (per the FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Gaps:** Many church registers in the fire zone were destroyed in October 1871; surviving pre-fire registers are those held by parishes outside the burn area or churches that subsequently reconstructed records
- **Language:** Most records in English; German, Polish, and other immigrant-community languages appear in ethnic parish registers

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 all available; critically, the 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the originals were in Washington, D.C. — this is the primary source for identifying families present before the fire (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **State/provincial census:** Illinois state censuses were taken in intercensal years; this survey did not confirm their survival or digitization from tool results
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1885) record deaths in the year preceding each census
- **Access:** Federal census records are indexed on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and FamilySearch; the 1870 is especially important as a pre-fire anchor

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions, naturalizations
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate and court records were largely destroyed; FamilySearch has 2 digitized volumes for Chicago — volume 009982110 covers reconstructed pre-fire Cook County Court Records 1865–1871 (38 images, **browse-only**, 0% name-indexed, must be browsed image by image) and volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (112 images, 41% name-indexed — indexed + images)
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) holds Cook County records post-1871; Cook County courthouse holds later originals
- **Note on naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; post-fire Cook County court records at IRAD-NEIU should be searched for immigrant families

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Township and range (rectangular survey — Illinois is a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Land and Property page was not retrieved during this survey; federal land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, mortgages; crucially, reconstructed deeds filed under the Burnt Record Act (1872), which required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire
- **Date range:** Post-fire deed re-registrations begin 1872; pre-fire deeds were largely destroyed
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; FamilySearch volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (41% indexed)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registration, bounty land warrants; Civil War records are especially relevant for men of enlistment age in the 1860s
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) at https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ provides online access to many military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Chicago has multiple large cemeteries serving immigrant communities; specific names and denominational affiliations were not confirmed by tool results in this survey
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/ covers many Cook County cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may be held by individual cemeteries or the Chicago History Museum

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had multiple daily newspapers during this period; specific titles and date ranges were not confirmed by a tool result in this survey
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com at https://www.newspapers.com/ provides online access to historical Chicago newspapers; the Newberry Library holds physical microfilm
- **Content value:** Fire-era news (survivor lists, missing persons notices, relief rolls), obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices — fire-era newspaper coverage is a primary substitute for destroyed vital records

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago was an inland destination; most immigrants arrived through East Coast ports (New York, Baltimore, Boston) or Great Lakes ports
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906 in any court of record, post-1906 through the INS); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization files at IRAD-NEIU for Cook County courts
- **Where held:** NARA at https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry.com passenger collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls were destroyed; post-fire records begin with the Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872)
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor's records; this survey did not confirm online availability
- **Substitute value:** Post-fire tax records can substitute for missing property documentation; pre-fire city directories serve as the primary substitute for missing census or tax years before 1871

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library — these are a critical pre-fire substitute, naming residents by address and occupation (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a key pre-fire substitute source for property ownership and family information (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)
- **Relief records:** Post-fire relief organizations documented displaced families; the Chicago History Museum may hold some of these records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collections 2024189 (births), 1913456 (deaths), 1756321 (marriages), 1803978 (church records); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records | Post-fire vital and church records; reconstructed pre-fire court records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 census records including the surviving 1870 pre-fire anchor | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records | Civil War and Spanish-American War service and pension files not in other collections | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Burial information and grave images where sexton records are not online | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Fire-era survivor and relief notices, obituaries, marriage announcements | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| NARA | National Archives collections | Immigration, naturalization, federal records | Mixed (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 total digitized volumes for Chicago in the searched range; both are detailed above and represent the complete matching set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories from 1840s, maps, manuscripts, historical materials | In-person research; some materials on microfilm |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records, photographs, personal papers, relief records | In-person research |
| IRAD-NEIU (Illinois Regional Archives Depository, Northeastern Illinois University) | Cook County records post-1871 including court, probate, and naturalization files | In-person or inquiry |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives for access |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Original vital records from 1871 onward | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1871 civil vital records (birth, death, marriage): destroyed in the fire; they do not exist
- Pre-fire probate and court files: destroyed; reconstructed copies where they exist are largely browse-only on FamilySearch or held physically at IRAD-NEIU
- City directories at the Newberry Library: not fully digitized online
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records: held physically at the Chicago History Museum, not available online
- Post-fire tax records: not confirmed as online in this survey
- Illinois state census records: survival and online status not confirmed in this survey

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, wiping out deeds, birth and death registers, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The Burnt Record Act of 1872 partially compensated for lost property records by requiring re-registration, and some church registers were reconstructed, but significant gaps remain for the pre-1871 period. The 1870 federal census and city directories at the Newberry Library survived.

## Research tips
- The 1870 federal census is the single most important pre-fire record for Chicago families, because its originals survived in Washington. Use it as your anchor before the fire (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- For property ownership before the fire, check the Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872) — FamilySearch volume 009982111 covers these reconstructed deed filings 1871–1880 and is 41% name-indexed.
- For daily life and addresses before 1871, the city directories at the Newberry Library (from the 1840s) are essential and largely irreplaceable for the pre-fire period (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- The Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum contain pre-fire property and sometimes family information unavailable elsewhere (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- Church records are the first substitute for destroyed civil vital records; search the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives for Catholic families, and each denomination's own archives for others; some pre-fire registers survived outside the fire zone.
- Newspaper accounts from October–December 1871 (and into 1872) may include survivor lists, missing persons notices, and relief roll documentation — search Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library for the Chicago Tribune and other period papers.

- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; FamilySearch volume 009982111 covers post-fire property re-recordings 1871–1880 (41% indexed)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registration, bounty land warrants; Civil War records are especially relevant for men of enlistment age in the 1860s
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) at https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 at https://www.fold3.com/ provides online access to many military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Chicago has multiple large cemeteries serving immigrant communities; specific names and denominational affiliations were not confirmed by tool results in this survey
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/ covers many Cook County cemeteries
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may be held by individual cemeteries or the Chicago History Museum

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago had multiple daily newspapers during this period; specific titles and date ranges were not confirmed by a tool result in this survey
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com at https://www.newspapers.com/ provides online access to historical Chicago newspapers; the Newberry Library holds physical microfilm
- **Content value:** Fire-era news (survivor lists, missing persons notices, relief rolls), obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices — fire-era newspaper coverage is a primary substitute for destroyed vital records

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago was an inland destination; most immigrants arrived through East Coast ports (New York, Baltimore, Boston) or Great Lakes ports
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at NARA; naturalization records (pre-1906 in any court of record, post-1906 through the INS); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization files at IRAD-NEIU for Cook County courts
- **Where held:** NARA at https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry.com passenger collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property tax
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls were destroyed; post-fire records begin with the Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872)
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor's records; this survey did not confirm online availability
- **Substitute value:** Post-fire tax records can substitute for missing property documentation; pre-fire city directories serve as the primary substitute for missing census or tax years before 1871

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library — these are a critical pre-fire substitute, naming residents by address and occupation (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Insurance records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum is a key pre-fire substitute source for property ownership and family information (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories; Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)
- **Relief records:** Post-fire relief organizations documented displaced families; the Chicago History Museum may hold some of these records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collections 2024189 (births), 1913456 (deaths), 1756321 (marriages), 1803978 (church records); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records | Post-fire vital and church records; reconstructed pre-fire court records | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 census records including the surviving 1870 pre-fire anchor | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records | Civil War and Spanish-American War service and pension files not in other collections | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Burial information and grave images where sexton records are not online | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Fire-era survivor and relief notices, obituaries, marriage announcements | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| NARA | National Archives collections | Immigration, naturalization, federal records | Mixed (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 total digitized volumes for Chicago in the searched range; both are detailed above and represent the complete matching set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories from 1840s, maps, manuscripts, historical materials | In-person research; some materials on microfilm |
| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records, photographs, personal papers, relief records | In-person research |
| IRAD-NEIU (Illinois Regional Archives Depository, Northeastern Illinois University) | Cook County records post-1871 including court, probate, and naturalization files | In-person or inquiry |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives for access |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Original vital records from 1871 onward | In-person or mail request |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1871 civil vital records (birth, death, marriage): destroyed in the fire; they do not exist
- Pre-fire probate and court files: destroyed; reconstructed copies where they exist are largely browse-only on FamilySearch or held physically at IRAD-NEIU
- City directories at the Newberry Library: not fully digitized online
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records: held physically at the Chicago History Museum, not available online
- Post-fire tax records: not confirmed as online in this survey
- Illinois state census records: survival and online status not confirmed in this survey

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, wiping out deeds, birth and death registers, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The Burnt Record Act of 1872 partially compensated for lost property records by requiring re-registration, and some church registers were reconstructed, but significant gaps remain for the pre-1871 period. The 1870 federal census and city directories at the Newberry Library survived.

## Research tips
- The 1870 federal census is the single most important pre-fire record for Chicago families, because its originals survived in Washington. Use it as your anchor before the fire (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire).
- For property ownership before the fire, check the Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872) — FamilySearch volume 009982111 covers these reconstructed deed filings 1871–1880 and is 41% name-indexed.
- For daily life and addresses before 1871, the city directories at the Newberry Library (from the 1840s) are essential and largely irreplaceable for the pre-fire period (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- The Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum contain pre-fire property and sometimes family information unavailable elsewhere (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories).
- Church records are the first substitute for destroyed civil vital records; search the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives for Catholic families, and each denomination's own archives for others; some pre-fire registers survived outside the fire zone.
- Newspaper accounts from October–December 1871 (and into 1872) may include survivor lists, missing persons notices, and relief roll documentation — search Newspapers.com and the Newberry Library for the Chicago Tribune and other period papers.

## Louisiana in the French Colonial Period (1700s)

Researching families in Louisiana during the 1700s means working in a colonial era that had **no civil registration at all**. The territory was French from 1699 to 1762, then Spanish until the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. During that entire period, the Catholic Church — the only legally recognized church under the colonial *Code Noir* — was the keeper of all vital records: baptisms, marriages, and burials.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**Catholic Church Registers**
- The best-surviving registers begin at **St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans** in 1720.
- Available on FamilySearch as an indexed collection: *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925*
- Also available as browse-only digitized volumes in French and Spanish (no name search — must be read image by image)

**Colonial Court & Notarial Records (Superior Council)**
- Includes notarial acts, land grants, estate inventories, and court proceedings
- Originals held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in New Orleans
- 149 images from 1699–1769 are on FamilySearch (browse-only)

**Records Still Offline — Archival Repositories Abroad**
- **French period:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France — holds colonial census rolls, French administrative correspondence, and military muster rolls
- **Spanish period:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville — holds comparable Spanish colonial records

---

### Critical Warnings

1. **Language barrier:** Everything is in **French or Spanish**. Fluency or a translator is essential. (The *translation* agent can assist with French colonial records.)
2. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana returned only generic content during this survey; it would be worthwhile to re-run a wiki search once those pages are more accessible.

---

### Recommended Next Step

Open a research plan targeting the specific family lines and parishes you are tracing, using this guide's record types and repositories as the starting framework. If you tell me the family surname(s) and parish area, I can help plan the specific searches.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Louisiana was claimed for France in 1682 by La Salle; New Orleans was founded in 1718. France ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain administered the colony until retroceding it to France in 1800; the United States acquired it in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of the Superior Council and Catholic diocese)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (French colonial empire); Province of Louisiana under Spanish rule after 1762
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by this survey's tools; the colony had a small European settler population concentrated around New Orleans, with a large enslaved African population.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco); fur trade; river commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Acadian refugees (from 1755 onward), Spanish colonial administrators, enslaved Africans, free persons of color, and Native American peoples
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic Church exclusively (the only legally recognized church under the Code Noir in French Louisiana)
- **Key historical events:** Code Noir (1724) required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons; Acadian expulsion and resettlement (1755–1769); Spanish assumption of control (effective 1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803)

## Boundary changes
- 1699–1762: Entire territory under French colonial rule (Superior Council at New Orleans)
- 1762: France ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau); eastern Louisiana to Britain
- 1769: Spanish effective governance began under Governor Alejandro O'Reilly
- 1800–1803: Secretly retroceded to France; sold to the United States 1803
- Records during the Spanish colonial period (1769–1803) are often still written in French but were administered through Spanish legal structures; both French and Spanish record series must be searched.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed during the colonial period (1700s). The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and does not state a civil-registration start date for Louisiana; that date cannot be confirmed from this survey's tool results.
- **What exists:** Catholic Church sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) served as the de facto vital records for all free colonists and, under the Code Noir, for enslaved persons. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720 (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Where held:** Originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral. FamilySearch holds a digitized but browse-only volume of Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803 (image group 004330991, 264 images, French/Spanish, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable). FamilySearch indexed collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) also covers this period.
- **Gaps:** Records predating 1720 are extremely sparse; records from parishes outside New Orleans may survive only in physical form at individual church archives.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Notarial records (Superior Council), estate inventories, and colonial census rolls at ANOM.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic Church exclusively (the Code Noir prohibited any other public religious practice). Acadian Catholic communities arrived from 1755 onward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral Archives and Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals). FamilySearch holds two digitized but browse-only volumes: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans (1720–1803, image group 004330991, 264 images) and French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records (1699–1769, image group 004330992, 149 images). Both are in French and Spanish and must be browsed image-by-image with no name index.
- **Language:** French (1699–1762 period) and French/Spanish (Spanish colonial period 1762–1803). Researchers must be able to read these languages.
- **Gaps:** No surviving parish registers from before 1720 were confirmed by this survey's tools. Rural parishes outside New Orleans may have only physical records.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** No federal census existed during the colonial period. The French colonial administration conducted periodic census rolls (recensements); these are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Post-statehood federal census:** The first federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 (after the Louisiana Purchase, 1803), outside the 1700s target window.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM are physical records; contact ANOM directly or use their online catalog.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, administration proceedings, guardianships — all processed through the Superior Council (the colonial court of record).
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, indexed, with images at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) covers the colonial period from 1756.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) holds original Superior Council records; some are partially digitized. FamilySearch collection 2078341 provides indexed access from 1756.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpents), inherited by Spanish administration; not the American rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French concessions and Spanish land grants. Colonial-era land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office (per the FamilySearch Wiki search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, mortgages, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s onward at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — one of the oldest continuous notarial offices in North America (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access, in-person). Louisiana State Land Office, Baton Rouge. FamilySearch volume 004330992 (French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records, 1699–1769, 149 images, browse-only, French).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763), Spanish colonial militia service (after 1769), American Revolution (some Louisiana militia involvement).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls and service records. This survey did not confirm digitized online access to colonial-era Louisiana military records.

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Guide (1850–1910)

**Focus county:** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), the heart of Pennsylvania's anthracite region. The same record types apply to neighboring **Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland** counties, each of which would need its own survey if research there is planned.

### Coal-Industry–Specific Records
These are the most distinctive records for mining families:

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County (1870–1900)** — 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch.

  - Lithuanian Catholic
  - (and other immigrant communities)

---

### Naturalization Records
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (not NARA), because miners naturalized in local courts of record before the 1906 federal reform.

---

### Census Records
- Federal census records (1850–1910) are available through FamilySearch and other repositories and are foundational for locating mining households, ages, birthplaces, and neighbors.

---

### Key Repositories
| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
