# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1850–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed in this survey's tool results
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned during this survey (place_population returned no data)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish Catholic, Welsh, Polish, and Lithuanian immigrant communities documented in ethnic parishes ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic
- **Key historical events:** State Mine Inspector annual reports published from 1870; United Mine Workers of America founded 1890

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811; boundaries appear stable through the target period
- Neighboring Lackawanna County separated from Luzerne County around 1878 — the volume_search returned Lackawanna volumes beginning that year; events in that area before 1878 were recorded under Luzerne County

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content and gave no Pennsylvania-specific vital registration start dates with levels. FamilySearch collection 2255317 ("Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968") begins in 1906, but no wiki page confirmed when statewide death registration was required.
- **What exists:** Death certificates from 1906 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images); county marriages from 1885 (collection 1921317, 524,189 indexed records); civil marriages from 1677 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records); compiled marriage index 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images). No indexed statewide birth certificate collection for the late 1800s was returned by this survey.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch for collections above; county courthouse for original registers
- **Gaps:** No indexed birth certificate collection for births before 1906 was returned; for births, church baptismal registers are the primary alternative
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers; Mine Inspector reports for deaths from mining accidents

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic — each served specific mining communities ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm; identifying the congregation is essential before searching, as registers are organized by parish, not county
- **Gaps:** No confirmed digitized Schuylkill County church record collection was returned by this survey (one entry in the collections_search was explicitly labeled a synthetic test fixture and is excluded from this guide)
- **Language:** Records of Polish and Lithuanian parishes will be in those languages

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Decennial enumerations 1850–1910 all cover this period; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/). The 1870, 1880, and 1900 schedules list occupation as "miner" for coal mining families ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** The generic wiki content mentions mortality schedules recording deaths in the year preceding each census; Pennsylvania-specific coverage was not confirmed in this survey
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not hold a state census; none returned for this period
- **Access:** Indexed and searchable via Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Date range:** Collection 1999196 ("Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994") covers this period
- **Access:** Browse-only images (3,200,560 images; 0% name-indexed) — must be browsed image by image with no search capability
- **Where held:** FamilySearch for browse-only images; Schuylkill County Courthouse for originals

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a metes-and-bounds state (not rectangular survey)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** No Pennsylvania-specific land office details were confirmed by this survey's wiki pages
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** County courthouse for deed books; Pennsylvania State Archives for earlier records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 for digitized military records (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is available for Schuylkill County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; Historical Society of Schuylkill County may hold transcriptions

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No specific Schuylkill County newspaper titles or date ranges were confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; local library or historical society for microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York — primary arrival ports for Irish and Eastern European miners ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (at NARA); naturalization records; Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for passenger lists; Pennsylvania State Archives for Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property
- **Where held:** County courthouse, Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing census years

### Other record types — coal mining specific
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County, 1870–1900):** Image group 002240015; 410 images; 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — the most accessible mining-specific digitized source for this county
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870–1895):** Image group 002240016; 287 images; browse-only — no name index
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878–1900):** Image group 002240017; 199 images; browse-only
- **Mine Inspector Annual Reports (from 1870):** State-published reports listing fatal accident victims by name, age, nationality, and cause of death; held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **UMWA membership rolls (from 1890):** United Mine Workers of America grievance files and membership rolls; held at local historical societies

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 2255317 (Death Certs, 1906-1968, 4.2M records); 1921317 (County Marriages, 1885-1950, 524K records); 1999196 (Probate Records, 1683-1994, browse-only); 1571957 (Civil Marriages, 1677-1950); 1502909 (Compiled Marriages index, 1700-1900) | Vital records, probate | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records not name-indexed on FamilySearch | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records not in vital record series | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, accident notices absent from vital records before 1906 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Service records for Civil War and Spanish-American War | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, federal naturalization post-1906 | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes match this place and period; the 3 detailed above under coal mining records are the first page of results. The remaining 20 volumes were not examined in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906); Mine Inspector annual reports; company employment records | In-person / written request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Local mining collections, local histories, company records | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community records for the anthracite region (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna) | In-person |
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Original deeds, court records, probate originals | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Birth certificates for the late 1800s — no indexed collection returned; church baptismal registers are the primary alternative
- Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) — at Pennsylvania State Archives, not in a confirmed online database
- Mine Inspector Annual Reports — held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies; digitization not confirmed
- UMWA membership rolls — held at local historical societies; online availability not confirmed
- Colliery payroll ledgers and company employment records — survive fragmentarily at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies
- Probate Records (collection 1999196) — images exist on FamilySearch but are browse-only with no name index

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Schuylkill County were confirmed by any tool result in this survey. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. Contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives directly to establish the fate of a specific record class.

## Research tips
- **Search the Mine Worker Employment Cards first:** Image group 002240015 covers Schuylkill County (1870–1900), is 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable, and is the most accessible digitized mining-specific source for adult males in this county ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).
- **Use Mine Inspector Annual Reports for deaths:** Published from 1870, these list every fatal accident victim by name, age, nationality, and cause of death — invaluable when death certificates predate statewide registration ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).
- **Identify the ethnic parish before searching church records:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, and Lithuanian Catholic parishes each served specific communities; registers are organized by congregation. Establishing the denomination is the prerequisite step.
- **Naturalization records are at the state archives, not NARA:** Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives because pre-1906 naturalizations were handled by any court of record ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).
- **Search neighboring anthracite counties:** Luzerne and Lackawanna counties are part of the same coal region; mining families crossed county lines. Lackawanna County records before 1878 were filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for that period.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content in this survey:** The Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Land and Property, and Probate Records pages all resolved to a generic article. Consult them directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki before relying on this guide's absence of Pennsylvania-specific registration dates.

- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** The generic wiki content mentions mortality schedules recording deaths in the year preceding each census; Pennsylvania-specific coverage was not confirmed in this survey
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not hold a state census; none returned for this period
- **Access:** Indexed and searchable via Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories
- **Date range:** Collection 1999196 ("Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994") covers this period
- **Access:** Browse-only images (3,200,560 images; 0% name-indexed) — must be browsed image by image with no search capability
- **Where held:** FamilySearch for browse-only images; Schuylkill County Courthouse for originals

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a metes-and-bounds state (not rectangular survey)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** No Pennsylvania-specific land office details were confirmed by this survey's wiki pages
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** County courthouse for deed books; Pennsylvania State Archives for earlier records

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 for digitized military records (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is available for Schuylkill County
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; Historical Society of Schuylkill County may hold transcriptions

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No specific Schuylkill County newspaper titles or date ranges were confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for digitized historical newspapers; local library or historical society for microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York — primary arrival ports for Irish and Eastern European miners ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (at NARA); naturalization records; Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) for passenger lists; Pennsylvania State Archives for Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax, personal property
- **Where held:** County courthouse, Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing census years

### Other record types — coal mining specific
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County, 1870–1900):** Image group 002240015; 410 images; 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable — the most accessible mining-specific digitized source for this county
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870–1895):** Image group 002240016; 287 images; browse-only — no name index
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878–1900):** Image group 002240017; 199 images; browse-only
- **Mine Inspector Annual Reports (from 1870):** State-published reports listing fatal accident victims by name, age, nationality, and cause of death; held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **UMWA membership rolls (from 1890):** United Mine Workers of America grievance files and membership rolls; held at local historical societies

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

| FamilySearch | Collection 2255317 (Death Certs, 1906-1968, 4.2M records); 1921317 (County Marriages, 1885-1950, 524K records); 1999196 (Probate Records, 1683-1994, browse-only); 1571957 (Civil Marriages, 1677-1950); 1502909 (Compiled Marriages index, 1700-1900) | Vital records, probate | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census records not name-indexed on FamilySearch | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records not in vital record series | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituaries, accident notices absent from vital records before 1906 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Service records for Civil War and Spanish-American War | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger lists, federal naturalization post-1906 | Free/In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes match this place and period; the 3 detailed above under coal mining records are the first page of results. The remaining 20 volumes were not examined in this survey.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |

| Pennsylvania State Archives | Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906); Mine Inspector annual reports; company employment records | In-person / written request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Local mining collections, local histories, company records | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton | Mining community records for the anthracite region (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna) | In-person |
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Original deeds, court records, probate originals | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Birth certificates for the late 1800s — no indexed collection returned; church baptismal registers are the primary alternative
- Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) — at Pennsylvania State Archives, not in a confirmed online database
- Mine Inspector Annual Reports — held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies; digitization not confirmed
- UMWA membership rolls — held at local historical societies; online availability not confirmed
- Colliery payroll ledgers and company employment records — survive fragmentarily at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies
- Probate Records (collection 1999196) — images exist on FamilySearch but are browse-only with no name index

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Schuylkill County were confirmed by any tool result in this survey. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. Contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives directly to establish the fate of a specific record class.

## Research tips
- **Search the Mine Worker Employment Cards first:** Image group 002240015 covers Schuylkill County (1870–1900), is 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable, and is the most accessible digitized mining-specific source for adult males in this county ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).
- **Use Mine Inspector Annual Reports for deaths:** Published from 1870, these list every fatal accident victim by name, age, nationality, and cause of death — invaluable when death certificates predate statewide registration ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).
- **Identify the ethnic parish before searching church records:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, and Lithuanian Catholic parishes each served specific communities; registers are organized by congregation. Establishing the denomination is the prerequisite step.
- **Naturalization records are at the state archives, not NARA:** Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives because pre-1906 naturalizations were handled by any court of record ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).
- **Search neighboring anthracite counties:** Luzerne and Lackawanna counties are part of the same coal region; mining families crossed county lines. Lackawanna County records before 1878 were filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for that period.
- **FamilySearch Wiki pages returned only generic content in this survey:** The Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Land and Property, and Probate Records pages all resolved to a generic article. Consult them directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki before relying on this guide's absence of Pennsylvania-specific registration dates.

Here is the locality guide for early Massachusetts Puritan research:

---

**Massachusetts, 1620–1700: Locality Research Guide** *(saved as loc_001)*

**Two Separate Colonies**
This period covers two distinct jurisdictions — **Plymouth Colony** (1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1630) — which remained separate until they merged in 1691. Their records are published and indexed independently, so it's important to know which colony your ancestor settled in.

**Key Record Types**

- **Town Vital Records** — Births, marriages, and deaths were required at the town level from **1639** onward. These are the most consistently surviving records for this era.
- **Congregational Church Registers** — Baptisms, memberships, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings. These are often the *only* records predating 1639, making them critical for the earliest settlers.
- **Probate Records** — Survive from the 1630s onward, held at county probate courts.
- **Deed and Land Proprietors' Records** — Held at county registries; important for tracing land transactions and family relationships.

**FamilySearch Collections (Confirmed)**
FamilySearch holds:
- Indexed collections for town vital records, church records, and probate records
- Two digitized but unindexed volumes:
  - Town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (browse image by image)
  - Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County, 1630–1700 (full-text searchable but not name-indexed)

**Key Repositories**
- **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** — Original colony records, court records, and governor's correspondence from the 1620s onward
- **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS, Boston)** — Holds the *Great Migration* study series, which documents every known settler who arrived between 1620 and 1643. **This is the essential first step** for anyone researching a potential Puritan ancestor.

**Recommended Next Steps**
1. If your ancestor may have arrived before 1643, consult the *Great Migration* study series first.
2. Identify the specific town where your ancestor settled.
3. Search that town's vital records and local Congregational church registers.
4. Follow with probate and land records for the same county.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony established 1628, with major Puritan settlement beginning 1630; both merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for 1620–1700. Wikipedia notes approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630–1640.
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, and trade — the dominant industries shaped which towns generated the most records
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; also Native American populations, small numbers of indentured servants and enslaved persons
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (Puritan) was the established church; scattered Baptist, Quaker, and Anglican congregations emerged from mid-century
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630–1640 (~20,000 settlers, per Wikipedia); King Philip's War 1675–1676 disrupted many communities and may have caused local record losses

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691) were entirely separate jurisdictions throughout most of this period; records must be searched in each separately
- Both merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691, near the end of this survey period
- County-level administrative divisions within Massachusetts Bay Colony were created during the 1640s–1680s and boundaries shifted; land and probate records are filed by county, requiring identification of which county a town belonged to at the time of an event

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by Massachusetts Bay Colony starting in 1639 — events before 1639 survive only in church records. [FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records; Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony]
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the town level, 1639 onward; some towns recorded events earlier
- **Where held:** Original town clerk records at town halls; FamilySearch collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (indexed + images, 3,456,789 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil registration existed during this period; coverage depends on individual town survival
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church records are the primary substitute before 1639; the published Tanner–Corbin series ("Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850") abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns [wiki search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (Puritan) predominant; scattered Baptist, Quaker, and Anglican congregations from mid-century
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments) — disciplinary records name people found in no other series [wiki search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]
- **Where held:** Many published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications [wiki search]; FamilySearch collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (indexed + images, 987,654 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657; volume 007612045 covers Congregational church admissions and baptisms for Suffolk County, 1630–1700 (121 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed — browse with text search aid)
- **Gaps:** Records of smaller congregations have not all survived; Baptist and Quaker records are more scattered
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790, well outside this period; no federal census records exist for 1620–1700
- **Other enumerations:** No confirmed colonial-era enumeration was returned by the tools. Town meeting records (volume 007612044, Massachusetts, 1620–1698, 188 images) may enumerate inhabitants and proprietors and serve as a partial substitute
- **Access:** Volume 007612044 is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image with no search aid

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, and guardianships
- **Date range:** Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts [wiki search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (indexed + images, 567,890 records), at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901; originals at Massachusetts county probate courts and Massachusetts Archives
- **Note:** Probate records for this period are among the richest sources for family relationships — heirs and their relationships to the deceased are routinely named

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town-level proprietary grants were the primary land-distribution mechanism; deeds were recorded at the county level from the 1630s [wiki search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records, deeds, grants, and patents; volume 007612044 covers town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620–1698 (188 images, browse-only, 0% indexed)
- **Date range:** Proprietary records begin with earliest settlements, 1620

Here is the locality guide for early colonial Massachusetts (1620–1700):

---

**Two Separate Colonies to 1691**
Massachusetts before 1691 consisted of two distinct colonies — **Plymouth Colony** (from 1620) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (from 1628) — that merged in 1691. A family from this era may have records in either archive, so it's important to know which colony your ancestor lived in.

---

**Civil Vital Records (Town Level)**
Massachusetts law required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639** — one of the earliest mandated civil registration systems in North America. These records are held **at the town level**, not centrally, and must be searched town by town. The published **Tanner-Corbin vital records series** is a key compiled resource for these records.

---

**Church Records**
**Congregational church records** are often the *only* surviving record for vital events in this period and are essential to search alongside town clerk records. FamilySearch holds some colonial-era Suffolk County Congregational baptisms, but that volume is not name-indexed and must be browsed image by image.

---

**Probate Records**
Probate records survive for many early settlers and can document family relationships. FamilySearch holds probate collections for this period.

---

**Key Repositories**
- **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) — the richest original colonial-era records
- **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** — holds extensive early Massachusetts material and publishes the *Great Migration* study series
- **FamilySearch** — holds digitized town vital records, church records, and probate records for this era; note that some volumes are unindexed and require image browsing

---

**Most Important Starting Point**
The **NEHGS Great Migration study series** profiles every known settler who arrived in New England from **1620–1643**. This is the essential first step for any Puritan-era ancestor — it will tell you what is known about the individual and point you to the original sources.

---

**Next Steps**
1. Identify the specific Massachusetts **town** the family lived in.
2. Search that town's entry in the **published vital records series**.
3. Check the **Great Migration volumes** at NEHGS.
4. Then move to original **town clerk and church records** in the archives.

## Massachusetts, 1620–1700: Records for Puritan-Era Research

This is one of the richest periods in American genealogy. Here's what you need to know:

### Two Colonies, Two Record Systems
Before the 1691 provincial charter merged them, **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691)** and **Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691)** each had separate courts, land systems, and record series. It's essential to know which colony your ancestor lived in.

### Civil Vital Records — The Earliest in North America
Massachusetts mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths from **1639 onward**. FamilySearch holds indexed collections covering this period:
- **Town vital records** — over 3.4 million entries
- **Church records** (mostly Congregational) — nearly 1 million entries
- **Probate records** — over 560,000 entries

Two additional digitized record sets are available but require browsing rather than name searching:
- Town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698
- Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630–1700

### Key Repositories & Resources
- **FamilySearch.org** — indexed collections noted above
- **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** at [americanancestors.org](https://americanancestors.org) — home of the *Great Migration* study series, which documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 and often traces English origins
- **FamilySearch Wiki** — check pages specific to Massachusetts record types for start dates and coverage gaps

1. Search the **Great Migration** volumes (NEHGS) for pre-1643 arrivals
2. Search FamilySearch's **Massachusetts Town Vital Records** collection
3. Check **probate records** for estate inventories naming children and neighbors

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628; Plymouth Colony established 1620. Province of Massachusetts Bay charter issued 1691, merging both colonies.
- **Administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Crown of England; from 1691, Province of Massachusetts Bay under royal charter
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this period. Wikipedia notes approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630-1640 alone.
- **Economy:** Agricultural settlements, fishing, fur trade, timber; shaped records through land grants and town proprietorships
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; small numbers of other Europeans; Indigenous communities whose land transactions appear in colonial records
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established church; small numbers of Quakers (persecuted and their records separate), Baptists, and Anglicans by late 1600s
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640 (~20,000 settlers, per Wikipedia); King Philip's War 1675-1676 (disrupted towns and records); 1691 Province charter merging colonies

## Boundary changes
- **1620-1691:** Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony were two distinct jurisdictions with separate record systems. Families near their shared boundary may have records in either series.
- **1691:** Province of Massachusetts Bay charter merged both colonies. After this date, records fall under a single provincial system, though Plymouth-era series continue as a distinct body of earlier records.
- Note: Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Researchers must search both even for families clearly in one colony, as movement between them was common.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated from **1639 at the town level** in Massachusetts Bay Colony (source: wiki_search result from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records, confirmed by Wikipedia on Massachusetts Bay Colony). There was no county or statewide civil registration in this period.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by town clerks; surviving records vary by town
- **FamilySearch collection:** Collection 2061550, "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" — 3,456,789 records with images, name-indexed; date range overlaps the full 1620-1700 period (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)
- **Published compilations:** The Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850 series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns, per wiki_search
- **Pre-1639 alternatives:** Passenger ship manifests, church records, and the Great Migration study series (see Church records below)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) as the established and by far dominant denomination; Congregational meetings were required for all residents regardless of personal faith
- **Record types:** Member admissions, baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments — these often name family relationships)
- **FamilySearch collection:** Collection 1921657, "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" — 987,654 records, date range overlaps the full period (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)
- **Digitized volume (browse/full-text):** Image group 007612045 — Congregational church admissions and baptisms, Suffolk County, 1630-1700; 121 images; **0% name-indexed but full-text searchable** (reachable via fulltext_search, not record_search); must be searched by keyword rather than name index
- **Published transcriptions:** Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications, per wiki_search (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Physical repositories:** Congregational church archives; Massachusetts Archives; New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Did not begin until 1790 — entirely outside the 1620-1700 period
- **Colonial enumerations:** No specific colonial enumeration volumes for Massachusetts were returned by volume_search for this period beyond the two volumes noted under church and town records
- **Substitutes:** Town tax lists and assessment records; town meeting minute books (see Town records below); proprietors' lists in land records

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, letters of administration, guardianships; county probate courts functioning from the 1630s, per wiki_search
- **FamilySearch collection:** Collection 1678901, "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" — 567,890 records, date range covers the full period (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)
- **Massachusetts General Court:** Colony-level court records from the 1620s onward held at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston), per wiki_search
- **Plymouth Colony:** Plymouth Colony court and probate records are published and indexed separately

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietorships were the primary mechanism for land distribution in both colonies; county registries of deeds recorded transfers from the 1630s, per wiki_search
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, proprietors' records, town allotments
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 007612044 — town meeting and proprietors' records, Massachusetts, 1620-1698; 188 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image, with no search capability**
- **Date range:** Deeds survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries from the 1630s, per wiki_search (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **Physical repository:** County registries of deeds; Massachusetts Archives for colony-level grants and patents

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War, 1675-1676 — the most significant armed conflict of this period in Massachusetts
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, pay records, town militia lists; pension and bounty land warrant records for this era are sparse
- **Physical repository:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colonial militia and war records; no specific digitized FamilySearch volume for this period was returned by volume_search
- **Note:** No FamilySearch collection specifically for 1620-1700 Massachusetts military records was returned by collections_search

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Burial grounds in every original Puritan town (Boston's Granary Burying Ground, 1660; King's Chapel Burying Ground, 1630; Plymouth's Burial Hill, 1620)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) carries transcriptions for many colonial-era Massachusetts burial grounds
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where they survive; most colonial-era burials are identified only from gravestone inscriptions

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Boston News-Letter (founded 1704) is the first continuously published colonial newspaper in America — entirely **after** most of the 1620-1700 period. No newspapers existed in Massachusetts during 1620-1700.
- **Substitute:** Colonial broadsheets, pamphlets, and published court proceedings held at the Massachusetts Archives and NEHGS

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** The 1620-1700 period predates systematic passenger list collection by the U.S. government (which began in 1820; FamilySearch collection 1784312, Passenger Lists 1820-1891, does not cover this period)
- **Great Migration records:** The Great Migration study series (published by NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving in Massachusetts 1620-1643, per wiki_search — this is the primary finding aid for immigrant origins
- **Ships' passenger lists:** 17th-century lists survive for some voyages and are published and indexed in the Great Migration volumes and separately in New England genealogical journals
- **Physical repository:** Massachusetts Archives; NEHGS; published in the Great Migration series
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town tax assessments and rate lists recorded at the town level
- **Substitute value:** Useful when vital records are absent; can confirm residence and approximate economic status in a given year
- **Physical repository:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town clerk offices; some published in local histories

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Image group 007612044, town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698, 188 browse-only images — these record town governance, land allotments, road assignments, poor relief, and other business that names residents otherwise absent from vital records
- **Massachusetts General Court records:** Colony legislature records from the 1620s onward at the Massachusetts Archives — name individuals in petitions, freeman admissions, and special proceedings
- **Freeman lists:** Admission as a freeman (voting member) of the colony required Congregational church membership; these lists name prominent heads of household and their religious affiliations
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early 20th-century published histories often reprint early records and are sometimes the only surviving transcription of records since lost

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 2061550) | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 — 3,456,789 records | Town-level births, marriages, deaths | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1921657) | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 — 987,654 records | Congregational baptisms, marriages, burials | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657 |
| FamilySearch (collection 1678901) | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 — 567,890 records | Wills, administrations, inventories | Free — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 |
| FamilySearch (image group 007612044) | Town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698, 188 images — browse-only | Land allotments, town governance, residence evidence | Free — browse-only, no name index |
| FamilySearch (image group 007612045) | Congregational church admissions and baptisms, Suffolk County 1630-1700, 121 images — full-text searchable | Suffolk County church membership and baptisms not in collection 1921657 | Free — full-text search only, not name-indexed |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Colonial burial grounds | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Fold3 | Military records | King Philip's War era service records | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA | National Archives holdings | Federal-level records (limited for 1620-1700) | In-person / online — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 2 total digitized volumes matching Massachusetts, 1620-1700 — both are detailed above; the returned page was the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, Massachusetts General Court records, governor's correspondence, court records from the 1620s onward | In-person; some records available on microfilm |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Great Migration study series 1620-1643; manuscript collections; published genealogies; largest genealogical library in New England | In-person; some online via americanancestors.org (subscription) |
| County registries of deeds | Deed books from the 1630s onward in remarkably complete runs | In-person at each county registry; some microfilmed |
| County probate courts | Probate files from the 1630s | In-person; original files at county level |

## Records NOT online
- Town tax assessment lists and rate books
- Massachusetts General Court records and petition files
- County court minute books (beyond indexed collections)
- Many individual church session books not included in collection 1921657
- Town meeting minute books not included in image group 007612044
- Plymouth Colony records (1620-1691) are published and indexed separately; not fully integrated into the FamilySearch collections above — search the published volumes at NEHGS

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Massachusetts, 1620-1700 were confirmed by tool results during this survey. The Massachusetts Archives holds the original colony records and states they survive from the 1620s onward. Consult the Massachusetts Archives directly for any gaps in specific town or court series.

## Research tips
- **Begin with the Great Migration study series** (NEHGS / americanancestors.org): it documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643, often with English origins, ship details, and early Massachusetts family data — it is the essential starting point for any 17th-century Massachusetts family (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Search Plymouth Colony records separately**, even for families clearly in Massachusetts Bay Colony territory. The two colonies' boundaries were porous and families crossed them. Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed separately.
- **Identify the specific town first.** All vital records were kept at the town level from 1639; a county or statewide search alone will not reach them. Use the Vital Records to 1850 series abstracts as the finding aid.
- **Congregational church records fill gaps that town vital records leave.** Member admission lists, disciplinary proceedings, and baptism registers often document family relationships and movements not found in civil records. For Suffolk County families, image group 007612045 is full-text searchable (keyword search, not name-indexed).
- **Town meeting minute books and proprietors' records** (image group 007612044, browse-only) name residents in land allotments, road maintenance assignments, poor relief decisions, and other civic matters — especially valuable when vital records are absent for a person.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki specific Massachusetts pages** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) returned only generic content during this survey. Consult those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki for Massachusetts-specific guidance before concluding a record type is unavailable.

### Two Distinct Jurisdictions
Research must follow **both** trails if your ancestor could have lived in either colony:

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; Plymouth Colony founded 1620 and operated separately until 1691, when both were merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay under a royal charter.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Governor John Winthrop led approximately 20,000 settlers in the Great Migration between 1630 and 1640 (per Wikipedia); no colonial census exists to give a precise figure for 1700.
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, lumber, coastal trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; indigenous Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and Narragansett nations throughout the region
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) established church; small Quaker meetings after 1656; Anglican minority
- **Key historical events:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1678) caused widespread destruction of towns and loss of records across central and western Massachusetts

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) operated as a wholly separate colony with its own government, courts, and vital-record system. Its records are indexed and published separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records.
- In 1691, Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay under a royal charter, unifying the record-keeping systems.
- For ancestors in Plymouth Colony towns (Plymouth, Duxbury, Barnstable, Marshfield, etc.) before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records as a separate research trail from Massachusetts Bay records.
- Massachusetts Bay County formation began in 1643 with Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk Counties. Land deeds and probate records follow county lines from that date; for events before 1643, the Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court records are the governing source.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town level — the Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639, one of the earliest civil vital-record mandates in North America (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Statewide (state-level) registration did not begin until 1842. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page was not accessible during this survey to confirm additional registration-level detail.
- **What exists:** Town clerk registers of births, marriages, and deaths from the 1630s onward, in varying completeness. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) covers this period and is searchable online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550.
- **Gaps:** King Philip's War (1675–1678) destroyed or damaged records in many towns; some towns did not begin recording until years after the 1639 mandate; early entries are sparse.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established and dominant church. Small Quaker meetings emerged after 1656. Anglican presence was minimal before 1700.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments), and burial records.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657. Originals are held by surviving congregations, with many deposited at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston), NEHGS, and local historical societies. Many have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational), Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy.
- **Gaps:** Not all early congregations kept systematic registers; some were lost in King Philip's War.
- **Language:** English.

One digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007612045, 121 images) covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms 1630–1700; it is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — it cannot be searched by name and must be accessed via text search.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Begins in 1790 — entirely outside this period.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No systematic colonial census survives for Massachusetts Bay for 1620–1700. Town meeting records, tax lists (town rates), and militia muster rolls serve as partial substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Proprietors' lists in town records enumerate landowning householders by name.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships.
- **Date range:** From 1635 for Massachusetts Bay counties; Plymouth Colony probate from the 1630s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901. Originals held at county probate courts and Massachusetts Archives. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Probate Records page was not accessible during this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors distributed land within each town; county registries of deeds recorded conveyances from the 1630s. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page was not accessible during this survey to confirm the granting office.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records, deeds, grants, mortgages.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (originals); Massachusetts Archives. One digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007612044, 188 images) covers town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 — browse-only images, not name-indexed, not full-text searchable.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1678). No federal military records exist for this period.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, pay lists, and council-of-war proceedings held in the Massachusetts Archives. Published transcriptions appear in the Massachusetts Historical Society Collections series.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); Massachusetts Historical Society.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burying grounds associated with Congregational meeting houses (e.g., King's Chapel Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1630; Granary Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1660).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many early Massachusetts cemeteries with transcribed inscriptions.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for the 17th century; gravestone inscriptions are frequently the only direct evidence of burial.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No sustained newspaper existed in Massachusetts before 1704 (Boston News-Letter). Newspapers are essentially unavailable as a source for 1620–1700.
- **Content value:** Not applicable for this period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary ports of entry.
- **Record types:** English port departure records (held in England); ship passenger lists reconstructed by historians. The Great Migration study (NEHGS) documents known arrivals 1620–1643 from multiple sources.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) covers only 1820–1891 and does not apply to the 1620–1700 period. For 17th-century arrivals, use the Great Migration study volumes (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS) and English records (State Papers, port books) available through Ancestry and FindMyPast.
- **Content note:** Colonial-era passenger lists are reconstructed from English and colonial sources, not from systematic American manifests (which did not exist). The full manifest of a ship record names all passengers including infants and children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rates (property and poll taxes) recorded in town meeting records.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Massachusetts Archives; some published in historical society series.
- **Substitute value:** A name in town rates confirms presence in the community at a specific date, substituting for census in the colonial period.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Minutes name every male taxpayer and record votes on local affairs, road maintenance, care of the poor, and land allotments — an indispensable source for colonial-period research.
- **Colony/General Court records:** The Massachusetts Bay General Court records (Massachusetts Archives) document laws, petitions, land grants, and judicial proceedings from the 1630s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (1678901) | Town-level vital, church, and probate records 1620–1700 | Free; https://www.familysearch.org |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Gravestone inscriptions where no burial register survives | Free; https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| NARA | General federal holdings | Federal records (mostly post-1700 for this region) | Free online / in-person; https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620–1700 — this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). Both are browse-only or full-text searchable but not name-indexed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, General Court records, colonial court records, vital records supplements from 1620s | In-person; catalog at www.sec.state.ma.us/arc |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration study series, vital records abstracts | In-person / subscription at americanancestors.org |
| County registries of deeds | Original deed books from the 1630s | In-person at each county registry |
| County probate courts | Original wills, inventories, administrations from the 1630s | In-person at each county courthouse |
| Massachusetts Historical Society, Boston | Published transcriptions of colonial records, town histories | In-person / online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Town meeting records (1620–1700): The one FamilySearch volume covering this period (image group 007612044) is browse-only — no name index, no full-text search.
- County court records (civil and criminal, 1630s–1700): Not systematically digitized or indexed for the colonial period.
- Plymouth Colony records: Published in multi-volume sets; check NEHGS and research libraries. Not fully searchable online.
- English departure records for Great Migration immigrants: Held in England (State Papers, port books); some accessible via Ancestry and FindMyPast English record collections.

## Known record losses
King Philip's War (1675–1678) destroyed town records, church registers, and local documents in many Massachusetts towns — particularly in the Connecticut River valley and central Massachusetts. No tool result in this survey pinpoints specific town registers lost. The Massachusetts Archives is the primary repository for surviving colonial-era records. Published town histories sometimes preserve transcriptions of records since lost.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts returned only generic content during this survey — they were not Massachusetts-specific. Consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy before relying on this guide's absence of their details.
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) is a separate jurisdiction. If your ancestor lived in Plymouth Colony towns before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records — published and indexed separately — before Massachusetts Bay records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational), "Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately."
- The Great Migration study by Robert Charles Anderson (NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving in New England 1620–1643, with citations to primary sources — it is the starting point for any early Massachusetts ancestor.
- The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner–Corbin) abstracts town clerk records for more than 200 Massachusetts towns and is frequently the most accessible transcription of colonial vital records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- Town meeting and proprietors' records (FamilySearch volume 007612044, browse-only images, 188 images, 1620–1698) name inhabitants not found in surviving vital or church registers — essential for the colonial period.
- Congregational church admission records are distinct from baptismal registers: adult members were formally admitted to full communion, creating a separate dated record sometimes years after baptism; search both series.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; Plymouth Colony founded 1620 and operated separately until 1691, when both were merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay under a royal charter.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Governor John Winthrop led approximately 20,000 settlers in the Great Migration between 1630 and 1640 (per Wikipedia); no colonial census exists to give a precise figure for 1700.
- **Economy:** Fishing, farming, lumber, coastal trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; indigenous Wampanoag, Nipmuc, and Narragansett nations throughout the region
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) established church; small Quaker meetings after 1656; Anglican minority
- **Key historical events:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1678) caused widespread destruction of towns and loss of records across central and western Massachusetts

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) operated as a wholly separate colony with its own government, courts, and vital-record system. Its records are indexed and published separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records.
- In 1691, Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay under a royal charter, unifying the record-keeping systems.
- For ancestors in Plymouth Colony towns (Plymouth, Duxbury, Barnstable, Marshfield, etc.) before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records as a separate research trail from Massachusetts Bay records.
- Massachusetts Bay County formation began in 1643 with Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, and Suffolk Counties. Land deeds and probate records follow county lines from that date; for events before 1643, the Massachusetts Bay Colony General Court records are the governing source.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town level — the Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639, one of the earliest civil vital-record mandates in North America (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). Statewide (state-level) registration did not begin until 1842. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Vital Records page was not accessible during this survey to confirm additional registration-level detail.
- **What exists:** Town clerk registers of births, marriages, and deaths from the 1630s onward, in varying completeness. FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records) covers this period and is searchable online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550.
- **Gaps:** King Philip's War (1675–1678) destroyed or damaged records in many towns; some towns did not begin recording until years after the 1639 mandate; early entries are sparse.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established and dominant church. Small Quaker meetings emerged after 1656. Anglican presence was minimal before 1700.
- **Record types:** Membership admissions, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments), and burial records.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657. Originals are held by surviving congregations, with many deposited at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston), NEHGS, and local historical societies. Many have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational), Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy.
- **Gaps:** Not all early congregations kept systematic registers; some were lost in King Philip's War.
- **Language:** English.

One digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007612045, 121 images) covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms 1630–1700; it is full-text searchable but not name-indexed — it cannot be searched by name and must be accessed via text search.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** Begins in 1790 — entirely outside this period.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No systematic colonial census survives for Massachusetts Bay for 1620–1700. Town meeting records, tax lists (town rates), and militia muster rolls serve as partial substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Proprietors' lists in town records enumerate landowning householders by name.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships.
- **Date range:** From 1635 for Massachusetts Bay counties; Plymouth Colony probate from the 1630s.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records) is online at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901. Originals held at county probate courts and Massachusetts Archives. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Probate Records page was not accessible during this survey.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors distributed land within each town; county registries of deeds recorded conveyances from the 1630s. The FamilySearch Wiki Massachusetts Land and Property page was not accessible during this survey to confirm the granting office.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' records, deeds, grants, mortgages.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (originals); Massachusetts Archives. One digitized FamilySearch volume (image group 007612044, 188 images) covers town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 — browse-only images, not name-indexed, not full-text searchable.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–1638); King Philip's War (1675–1678). No federal military records exist for this period.
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, pay lists, and council-of-war proceedings held in the Massachusetts Archives. Published transcriptions appear in the Massachusetts Historical Society Collections series.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); Massachusetts Historical Society.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burying grounds associated with Congregational meeting houses (e.g., King's Chapel Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1630; Granary Burying Ground, Boston, est. 1660).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for many early Massachusetts cemeteries with transcribed inscriptions.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for the 17th century; gravestone inscriptions are frequently the only direct evidence of burial.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No sustained newspaper existed in Massachusetts before 1704 (Boston News-Letter). Newspapers are essentially unavailable as a source for 1620–1700.
- **Content value:** Not applicable for this period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary ports of entry.
- **Record types:** English port departure records (held in England); ship passenger lists reconstructed by historians. The Great Migration study (NEHGS) documents known arrivals 1620–1643 from multiple sources.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) covers only 1820–1891 and does not apply to the 1620–1700 period. For 17th-century arrivals, use the Great Migration study volumes (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS) and English records (State Papers, port books) available through Ancestry and FindMyPast.
- **Content note:** Colonial-era passenger lists are reconstructed from English and colonial sources, not from systematic American manifests (which did not exist). The full manifest of a ship record names all passengers including infants and children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town rates (property and poll taxes) recorded in town meeting records.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices and Massachusetts Archives; some published in historical society series.
- **Substitute value:** A name in town rates confirms presence in the community at a specific date, substituting for census in the colonial period.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting records:** Minutes name every male taxpayer and record votes on local affairs, road maintenance, care of the poor, and land allotments — an indispensable source for colonial-period research.
- **Colony/General Court records:** The Massachusetts Bay General Court records (Massachusetts Archives) document laws, petitions, land grants, and judicial proceedings from the 1630s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (1678901) | Town-level vital, church, and probate records 1620–1700 | Free; https://www.familysearch.org |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions | Gravestone inscriptions where no burial register survives | Free; https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| NARA | General federal holdings | Federal records (mostly post-1700 for this region) | Free online / in-person; https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620–1700 — this is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). Both are browse-only or full-text searchable but not name-indexed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, General Court records, colonial court records, vital records supplements from 1620s | In-person; catalog at www.sec.state.ma.us/arc |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration study series, vital records abstracts | In-person / subscription at americanancestors.org |
| County registries of deeds | Original deed books from the 1630s | In-person at each county registry |
| County probate courts | Original wills, inventories, administrations from the 1630s | In-person at each county courthouse |
| Massachusetts Historical Society, Boston | Published transcriptions of colonial records, town histories | In-person / online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Town meeting records (1620–1700): The one FamilySearch volume covering this period (image group 007612044) is browse-only — no name index, no full-text search.
- County court records (civil and criminal, 1630s–1700): Not systematically digitized or indexed for the colonial period.
- Plymouth Colony records: Published in multi-volume sets; check NEHGS and research libraries. Not fully searchable online.
- English departure records for Great Migration immigrants: Held in England (State Papers, port books); some accessible via Ancestry and FindMyPast English record collections.

## Known record losses
King Philip's War (1675–1678) destroyed town records, church registers, and local documents in many Massachusetts towns — particularly in the Connecticut River valley and central Massachusetts. No tool result in this survey pinpoints specific town registers lost. The Massachusetts Archives is the primary repository for surviving colonial-era records. Published town histories sometimes preserve transcriptions of records since lost.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts returned only generic content during this survey — they were not Massachusetts-specific. Consult them directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy before relying on this guide's absence of their details.
- Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) is a separate jurisdiction. If your ancestor lived in Plymouth Colony towns before 1691, search Plymouth Colony records — published and indexed separately — before Massachusetts Bay records. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational), "Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately."
- The Great Migration study by Robert Charles Anderson (NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving in New England 1620–1643, with citations to primary sources — it is the starting point for any early Massachusetts ancestor.
- The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner–Corbin) abstracts town clerk records for more than 200 Massachusetts towns and is frequently the most accessible transcription of colonial vital records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- Town meeting and proprietors' records (FamilySearch volume 007612044, browse-only images, 188 images, 1620–1698) name inhabitants not found in surviving vital or church registers — essential for the colonial period.
- Congregational church admission records are distinct from baptismal registers: adult members were formally admitted to full communion, creating a separate dated record sometimes years after baptism; search both series.

**Oklahoma & the Land Run of 1889 — Locality Guide**

Oklahoma was an almost entirely new place in 1889. Before the Land Run of April 22 that year, the western half was federally controlled **Unassigned Lands** with no county government, and the eastern half was **Indian Territory** governed by the Five Civilized Tribes under a separate federal framework. The most valuable records for Land Run-era families are:

**Key Record Types & Repositories**

- **Homestead Files** — the most direct source. Held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. under Record Group 49; partially searchable on FamilySearch and at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). These name the settler, their witnesses, and their proof of five years' continuous residence.
- **1890 Oklahoma Territorial Census** — the single most important early census source. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally, but the Oklahoma territorial census survives at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.
- **County marriages from 1890 onward** — searchable on FamilySearch.
- **Mission and church records (1820–1965)** — searchable on FamilySearch.
- **Indian Censuses and Rolls (1851–1959)** — essential for anyone with Five Civilized Tribes ancestry; searchable on FamilySearch.

**Two Critical Distinctions**

1. **Oklahoma Territory vs. Indian Territory**: These were entirely separate jurisdictions until statehood in 1907. Which record series you search depends on exactly where your ancestor settled — western (Territory) or eastern (Indian Territory) Oklahoma.
2. **Follow the trail backward**: Most Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, or Missouri**. The paper trail before 1889 almost always runs through one of those departure states rather than Oklahoma itself.

**Next Steps**

Identify which part of Oklahoma your ancestor settled in and which county they lived in by 1900, then search the homestead files and the 1890 territorial census as the first documentary anchors. The guide has been saved to your project as **loc_001**.
